speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Prime Minister to return to the question of the discussions he had with Mr. Kosygin concerning the matter of emigration from the Soviet Union and also the question of the rights of Jews and other cultural groups in the Soviet Union. speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):

speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker. The statements made by Mr. Kosygin in the committee, and, indeed, repeated in part at the press conference, were more or less in the same form as the statement he made to me, although he did not elaborate to me on statistics as he did, I believe, in the statement made to the committee of the House. However, it was generally couched in the same terms, namely, that he did not recognize that there were particular forms of discrimination against any of the Soviet people. He explained in what circumstances some Jews were not given the facilities to emigrate to Israel, but he stated that generally, and we concurred from the knowledge we have, there has been vastly increased emigration from the Soviet Union to Israel in the past little while, and I expressed the hope that this would continue.
On the problem of reunification of families, I pointed out very carefully to him that I was raising this matter merely on a humanitarian basis and that, as with other subjects, I was not trying to interfere in the internal affairs of their country but I was appealing to him on a humanitarian basis to further the cause of those who had made application for the reunification of families. I attempted somewhat to see if there were any reasons of policy or of doctrine as to why this subject had not met with more notable success and he assured me that there were not. It was essentially a matter of processing these names, of contacting the people and getting them through the bureaucracy and, in some cases, of discovering that those who had been applied for as subject, for reunification did not always want, when they were reached, to be reunited with the people on this side who wanted to be reunited with them. He said that there were some occasions when this happened. Generally, however, he expressed regret that the matter had taken some little time. He assured me that the names were in the works
(Mr. Trudeau.]

now, that he would see to it personally that substantial advance would be made on this subject.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ELIGIBILITY TO OLD AGE SECURITY OF PERSONS 60 TO 65 YEARS OF AGE
speechtext:
-This House regrets that the government has not deemed advisable to provide old age security pensions to persons between the ages of 60 and 65, or to the wife of a retired person, whatever the age. Any pension so awarded should be such as to enable anyone to live as decently as the physical, material and human resources of Canada would allow.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the days allotted to the opposition are a unique opportunity for us of the Social Credit Party of Canada to draw the attention of the government on ticklish matters with which the government does not dare deal in order to reach a rational solution.
This motion, which could be entitled "Adjustment of pensions for older Canadians", reads as follows:
-This House regrets that the government has not deemed advisable to provide old age security pensions to persons between the ages of 60 and 65, or to the wife of a retired person, whatever the age.. Any pension so awarded should be such as to enable anyone to live as decently as the physical, material and human resources of Canada would allow.
But if we accept the principle that Canada is one of the wealthiest countries in the world, I fail to see why we should trail far behind those same countries with regard to the social security of those who built our country.
In the past, it was difficult enough to set, according to accepted standards, the minimum age entitling one to a pension. If we refer to the Internation Labour Conference of 1932, the minimum age was not to exceed 65, but it took Canada 35 years to recognize the recommendation of the International Labour Office. Indeed, it was only in 1952 that universal old age security pensions provided for a uniform payment of $40 a month to everyone 70 or over. That was a very timid start considering the fact that in 1937, 30 years before Canada, Denmark lowered pensionable age to 60.
Since January 1, 1971, a 65 year old person gets a pension of $80 per month and if that person has no other source of income, he may be entitled to a $55 monthly supplement. We lost in terms of universality what we gained in terms of social assistance. In other words, the old age pension is no longer strictly a pension, but is partly social welfare. And that is precisely what people do not accept any more. I shall come back to this subject a little later.
It is absolutely essential for us to base our social reforms on economic requirements. In these days of
8890

October 21, 1971
Old Age Security Pensions
unemployment, the public opinion calls for the lowering of the retirement age, so that a greater number of people withdraw from the labour market, thus enabling younger people to find employment. Besides, that is the main reason why the government of Denmark reduced the eligible age for pension to 60 years in 1937.
In 1911, New Zealand set the pensionable age at 60. They even set eligibility at 55 for women.
In Australia, as early as 1910, the minimum eligible age for a pension was also lowered to 60.
In Canada, we had to wait until 1927 before persons 70 years and over were guaranteed payment of a miserable pittance of $20. It is so ridiculous that I am ashamed of stating the amount of the pension. Could not Canada which ranks among the ten richest countries in the world at least follow the example of the countries I have just mentioned?
Today, we urge the present government to give all older Canadians a pension based on the cost of living. I did say a pension, not the semblance of one such as the scheme that now exists. Pensions are dues, not social welfare. I am convinced that our country is rich enough to give good protection to those who spent the best years of their lives making their country progress. A pension that will reestablish social distributive justice, because it will not allow any patronage and will not result in any discrimination since all people will get the guaranteed minimum regardless of their social or monetary status.
How much would such a pension cost the Canadian treasury? Not more than we are spending today for bureaucracy and patronage of all kinds. Think of the millions the Canadian treasury is now spending to fight unemployment, for instance, for training, second training, third training, to support all the young people who, having finished their studies or their training, can still find no jobs.
Transferring funds allocated to workers 60 to 65 years old to government pensions will increase old age pension disbursements but at the same time and perhaps to a greater extent it will reduce funds allocated to support these unemployed persons or train them. It must be recognized that a family of unemployed individuals costs the government much more than a married couple receiving a pension.
I can, Mr. Speaker, give a simple example to illustrate what I have in mind. What happens to a factory worker who has reached retirement age? This factory worker, who is a breadwinner, will leave a fairly remunerative job to make room for whom? For another breadwinner who was unemployed. That is to say, the state was providing a living to this breadwinner who had perhaps three, four, five or six children, therefore costing the welfare bureau or the unemployment insurance-mostly the welfare bureau-$250, $300 or perhaps $350 a month. The latter will replace the other breadwinner, the retired one, in the last case and in the present situation the government would pay $255 a month.
That is why I said a moment ago that by giving a pension to those who reach age 60, the government will be called upon to spend more money, but in a number of cases, it would make a saving. On the other hand, in

granting this pension to all and without investigation, as is done now in the case of family allowances, the various provincial inquiries would be eliminated; these cost to the treasury as much as the income supplement which 35 per cent of pensioners receive on account of their poverty. In considering these two points only, we see that our case is justified.
We finally ask that the wife receive the same pension as her husband when the latter reaches retiring age and we base our request on the most elementary sense of justice. Let us consider the family as it exists in our Canadian society. The salary of the breadwinner is still that of the father. When he was at work, he was supporting the family economy and when he paid his taxes, he was doing so as the head of the family. Is it not true that when he ceases to receive his salary, it is the head of the family who loses his income? If a pension is to replace this salary, is it not logical that such pension be granted to a breadwinner? Otherwise, how can the father continue to carry out his role of head of the household without the financial means required for this?
I was going to suggest, as a solution to the problem, that the legislation be amended with regard to the family head. But there is a much simpler way: give the same pension to his spouse, whatever her age. In this way we would reach our objective, that is a guaranteed family income, and to all couples without exception.
Some may object to this, arguing that the rich do not need the old age pension. I would answer that they may not need it but that they are entitled to it, like all other citizens, because this is a pension and not social assistance.
That is why, at the beginning of my speech I established a distinction between a pension and assistance. One does have the right to a pension when perhaps one does not need it, but one is not entitled to any aid which one does not need. That should be quite clear. And I say that the pension should be universal because I consider that the worker has a right to it when he reaches 60. As for the money that one not needing it will receive, you can rest assured that it will quickly go back to where it came from, that is the national treasury, through income tax.
Since the old age security pension is taxable, all the inspectors in every Canadian income tax office will see to it to collect what is due. One must choose the lesser of two evils.
It would be better to have only one collection office, since the present financial system requires it. The cases of all taxpayers will have to be settled instead of the thousands of offices being maintained, which give rise to so many complaints and injustices and where the worst patronage since the heyday of the Taschereau regime is often rampant.
If time allowed me, I would quote hundreds of cases that I had to deal with in my riding, due to on the one hand, this guaranteed income supplement and, on the other hand, because the wife was too young when her husband reached retirement age.

Furthermore, there are conflicts of jurisdiction about the sharing of responsibilities in certain social fields. In Quebec, the situation is further complicated by a rather vague legislation in the field of social affairs, and mainly with regards to shared cost programs, to which the federal government contributes 50 per cent without having a say in the matter. It must also be said that provincial and federal regulations made by officials often supersede the law. Finally, all mothers have seen their cheque reduced to nil with the introduction of the guaranteed income supplement. That is the limit! The finest social mess in the world! Those are the situations that a member must face in his constituency.
The last part of our motion reads as follows: "Any pension so awarded should be such as to enable anyone to live as decently . . We still say according to the cost of living index, which would mean about $150 per month at the present time.
I know that all the officials associated with our rotten financial system will say that we are putting it on, since they are the ones who conceive, draw up and complicate the legislation introduced in this House. But do they remember sometimes their yearly salary of $24,000, $25,000, $30,000 or more, while the government states that when it gives $1 to a citizen, it must collect $3 in taxes? I know why.
It is well understood that they will never appreciate the sorry plight of pensioners, when they spend their lifetime in the unequalled luxury of their office, surrounded by secretaries who even fetch them a glass of water.
How can popular social legislation be expected from such bureaucrats? All these high officials should have to live for three years on the older people allowance and share their living quarters, I am sure that we would then get much better social legislation.
I am always surprised, when a bill is tabled in the House, to see all Liberal members without exception endorse the bill without having even read it. I am doubly surprised when the opposition dares to point out the shortcomings of the measure, to see these same Liberals howling against the opposition, charging it with filibustering in the House. However, like all of us, these same Liberal members must receive letters of protest from their constituents. Just like us, they must go through their riding to check the effects that legislation adopted by the House has on their constituents. It is not enough to adopt laws, it is more important to go in the field and see how they are accepted by the people, what are their good and ill effects and to come back here to move the appropriate amendments. And that is what all Social Credit members do in their riding every weekend.
It is just too easy to excuse oneself by blaming the local employees who do everything possible but who are very often overwhelmed by all those laws one would often believe had been invented to make things more difficult for them and to confuse people more. The employees who work close to the people always get the kicks the top men would have well deserved. At times, I have felt that might be the purpose of new social laws: to make people quarrel, that they might no longer have the time or opportunity to notice the administrative blunders of the governments.
Old Age Security Pensions
I shall now deal with the pensioners. I still have a few moments left, which I should like to use to pinpoint real cases, and the problems facing those people.
I have here files on some ten cases, but I could have brought along hundreds of them concerning people who are having problems with the Old Age Pensions Act. I apologize for not giving any names, because it could hurt those people. But that will help me point out the deficiencies of the present law and the problems that can plague a member seeking to solve all those difficulties with which he is confronted day in and day out.
First we have the latest device of the government: the guaranteed income supplement. I think that most of the correspondence we have received these last few months deals mainly with the guaranteed income from the 1st of January, when the pension was first raised by the incredible amount of 58 cents per month.
How many headaches this guaranteed income has given pensioners, who had always been under the impression that they were going to receive $135 a month-which turned out not to be the case at all. It seems as if great pains are taken to mislead the population in order to throw even more confusion and to create quarrels between members and their constituents-who presumably elected this member because they trusted him, and, quite naturally, turn to him when they have problems.
I think that all acts nowadays are meant to make the members' task harder and cause them even more problems. Let us take, for instance, the guaranteed income in the case of a couple in which the wife is not yet eligible to a pension. Before the supplement was introduced, the aged head of a household used to receive $79.42, while his wife received social security payments of-and I have the papers here to show it-between $1 and $75. In most cases, the wife receives $69, $70 or $72. As soon as the government introduced the garanteed income supplement, the father, who had no income as his wife was drawing social security benefits from Quebec, got $135. In Quebec the wife is no longer eligible to anything in that province from the moment when that father gets $135. Indeed I wrote several times to Mr. Castongay and he answered me that this was not possible, because it was absolutely necessary that he should get about the same amount he was getting before the increase.
Finally the government of Quebec acknowledged that that married couple needed $150, $155 or $160 to live and, since the government gave $135 to the husband, it immediately withdrew any assistance given to the wife.
There were dozens of such cases, Mr. Speaker, and that situation was called "the scythe" by the women who were too young to get the federal pension. And all those women believed and hoped that they would get the same pension so that they would at least come under the same government plan. And they were right. In fact they said: If my husband belongs to the federal government plan, I should at least belong to it too. We have jobs and it happens that I come under the provincial government plan whereas my husband belongs to the federal government plan.
That is absurd. That is why I said just now, Mr. Speaker, that there must absolutely be some justice and logic in

Therefore, it means he will have to live on $80 a month. That is what happens. An older married couple must live on $80 a month because there has been an increase which prompted Quebec to withdraw the $30 or $35 the spouse was getting. The couple must go through twelve months on $80 a month. As some would put it, it is no sinecure.
That is why I call the attention of the House on that matter. Once the husband is no longer eligible for unemployment insurance benefits, it is possible to determine his yearly budget two or three months in advance. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ELIGIBILITY TO OLD AGE SECURITY OF PERSONS 60 TO 65 YEARS OF AGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) upon bringing before the House the motion we are discussing and for the very human way he talked about the subject it covers. We think far too little about the older people of this country. Many people say, "Why, there are lots of old people around. There are more older people than ever before in this country." There have been many scientific changes during the century and many scientific advances. Each basic discovery has led to many other basic discoveries. More scientists are alive today than the combined total of all the other scientists who have lived since the world began. Never before in history, however, has there been such an awareness of the needs and attributes of youth, and never before has any society done so much to assess the needs of youth and to give them a free hand on the rudder of democracy. Yet, in all regions of the country it is the old who multiply more quickly than the rest of the population. Their numbers are increasing at break-neck speed.
For instance, when the Mayflower landed in Massachusetts in 1620, the population of the whole world stood at around 500 million. Today that is the population of one nation, India. Let us take a look back in time. Approximately 25,000 years ago there were 3 million people in the whole world. Ten thousand years ago there were 5 million people in the world. In other words, in over 15,000 years the human population had not even doubled. At the beginning of the Christian era the world population was only 150 million, much less than the population of the United States today. At the beginning of this century, the world population was just over one billion. In 1950 it approached three billion and by the year 2,000 the statisticians tell us it will be well over five billion. As a consequence of overcrowding, pollution, economics and insufficient space in which to stand, the problem is that these people will be aging fast, although the life expectancy is increasing. From 1940 to 1960 the world population grew by just over 1.5 per cent per year, but in the older age group, those over 60, it grew by 2.5 per cent. Statisticians tell us we are getting close to, if we are not already there, a population of 300 million people in the 60 year age group and over, more than the total population of the North American continent today.
The increase in the population of the aged is due to the containment of diseases by scientific medicine. The acute diseases have been brought under control so that the common cause of death in respect of people up to age 40 is accidental. There are many more people who reach age 40 only to find then that the aging and chronic diseases set in. These are the diseases that we have been unable to treat as successfully as those of the acute kind. These diseases which take their toll are heart disease, strokes, cancer, nephritis, respiratory diseases and arthritis. Many of the people who are suffering from these diseases are working today or trying to until they reach the calendar age of 65. Many people reach this age in good mental and
October 21, 1971

physical health. The crudest thing in the world is to stop them contributing to their own physical well-being and to the economics of this country. I am sure all of us in this House know of the contribution being made by people of 65 years of age and over. However, thousands of people suffering from chronic disease go to work daily simply so that they might obtain a larger pension at 65. They work under stress and strain.
I think it is about time that we assessed the physical and mental condition of people rather than considered their calendar age. They feel they must work because they know that every day their pension is being eroded. They know it will have less purchasing power. They know hidden taxes will take more of it. They are afraid to quit. They have strokes and coronaries at age 40 and at age 50. Provision should be made so that they would have a pension not at the calendar age of 60 or 65 but at the physical and mental age they represent. There is no question but that there was discrimination when the government brought in the old age supplement of $55 per month for a single person and $95 a month for a married couple with no other cash income. There certainly is discrimination and it is this I should like to see cured. I am in agreement with what the hon. member for Roberval said, but I also realize that, considering our economic position, we probably first want to correct the injustices that already exist in some areas and modernize the system.
But what about, say, John Brown who is partially disabled and owns a little house? He has a small pension of $80 per month from other sources, but he does not qualify for a disability pension or even for medicare. His wife is gone. He will receive only $80 a month, the purchasing power of which will diminish month by month because of inflation. There is nothing to compensate him. We stopped that, so actually we give the old age pensioner less every month. There are hundreds of John Browns who cannot make ends meet. They have been discriminated against. This particular man also has a heart condition and requires medication costing around $10 per month. The discriminating action of this government will not be forgotten. This magnanimous government, in a just society, increases the old age pension by 42 cents per month and then freezes it. These people will not forget that. Then, the pension is eroded by inflation caused largely by the poor management of this government.
Many widows are in the same position. They have a little home and a small pension. The pensions were smaller in the early days, but from 1948 to the present time the value of the dollar has decreased by 50 per cent. This is an indication of how the pension has been cut. I believe this Parliament has a responsibility in this regard. The old people should not be the forgotten people. There are very few elderly affluent people in the age bracket of 60 to 65 and over. They will remember the magnanimity of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in the next federal election. The rich old age pensioner really is non-existent, and the Prime Minister must remember that those people of 65 years of age represent 17 per cent or 18 per cent of the voting power of this country.
It is really the second part of the motion presented to the House that is the most interesting. It reads:
Old Age Security Pensions
Any pension so awarded should be such as to enable anyone to live as decently as the physical, material and human resources of Canada would allow.
I believe all of us-and I suggest this applies to all parties in the House-should wholeheartedly endorse that proposal. If any member of this House does not endorse it, I should like him to take part in this debate and explain his reason. There is a constant concern on this side of the House that the Liberal government has continually eroded the status and well-being of Canadian pensioners and has repeatedly ignored the plea for more adequate and meaningful assistance. Consequently, it is really the second part of the motion to which I wish to direct most of my attention.
Before I do so, however, I should like to comment on the part of this motion which calls for a reduction in the age level now required for eligibility for old age pensions. The motion calls for the inclusion of persons aged 60 to 64, and persons of any age who are spouses of pensioners. Again I say this is a noble gesture and one for which I have a great deal of sympathy. When medicare was discussed in this House reference was made to supplementary payments for drugs. This proposal was contained in the Hall Commission Report which was tabled in this House some four years ago, but that recommendation has never been carried out.
Let me say that once a person reaches 60 years of age his drug bill increases by four or five times, so that some of these people require up to $30 a month for drugs. However, this government does nothing to help those people who have difficulty meeting their drug bills. There are so many areas of unfairness that have been left in this scheme that I should like to see it modernized and brought up to date. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) has spoken from time to time about the guaranteed income, but then he shied away from that. Later, he told us of another plan which would bring the income of the old age pensioner close to that of a guaranteed income. I do not believe he knows what he means at all. This government just does not have any feeling or humanity, although I am sure they have these qualities individually. Why do they not get together over there and do a little thinking about such things as drug bills?
I will tell you something about the cost of drugs. Last year Canadians paid $271 million for drugs. If you take 17 per cent of 23 million people which is the percentage of the population over 60, you realize there is one person in 12 or one person in 13, in that category. Since these elderly people use drugs four times oftener than those under 60, you can see how much money those older people require. The federal government should establish a scheme to cover drug costs, similar to the national medicare scheme so the provinces could follow suit. This is not just my own idea. There is an election in Ontario today. Perhaps I should not mention that, but it is expected that the cost of drugs will be covered in the province of Ontario. Of course, we all know that election promises do not always become law, but I hope that such a bill will be introduced.
Another piece of legislation that was introduced-we have moved in this direction but we are moving so slowly-is one that would cover the cost of patients in

October 21, 1971
Old Age Security Pensions
nursing homes, with the exception of $3 per day. This is a big thing. We have done something in this direction but there are still many pockets of people who have been forgotten. Over 500,000 Canadians over 65 are in this category. This is why I plead with the government to get off its seat. I know that on many occasions, Mr. Speaker, you have been lenient with me when I was asking the Minister of National Health and Wefare questions, but I also know that you have realized his answers were neither up to date nor very helpful in assisting us to ascertain the real situation.
In pleading for the older people I want to say that boredom, alienation, poor health and reduced incomes are their main problems. The problems of the older people receive very little attention in the press. How many stories do you hear concerning them compared to those about younger people? They get no notice on the CBC, and this is amazing. How many times, Mr. Speaker, have you seen a program about older people and how they live? Reference was made to this point by the hon. member for Roberval when he cited case histories. How many times have we heard about these people? If the views of older people are rarely heard on the CBC, on radio or television, it is because most of the performers, and indeed the programs, are slanted towards sports, culture and styles in the arts. The older people are just not mentioned. This is not just my observation. A member of this House who had the honour of being the postmaster general appeared before the Senate Committee and stated that there were no programs aimed specifically at representing the plight of the older people in Canada. When one considers that over 500,000 old age pensioners are on incomes between $1,320 and $4,500, which is below the poverty line, one realizes the gravity of the problem.
Again I compliment the hon. member for Roberval who so thoughtfully brought in this motion and thus brought these problems to the attention of the government. In my own way, I have brought to the attention of the government the plight of older people. The world is getting older by the day. When I look around me, and at hon. members opposite, I realize that most of us are approaching the age of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, arthritis and respiratory diseases.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ELIGIBILITY TO OLD AGE SECURITY OF PERSONS 60 TO 65 YEARS OF AGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to commend the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) on the introduction of the motion that is now before the House. We shall be pleased to give it our full support. As I see it, the motion is in two parts. In the first half of it the hon. member requests that consideration be given to the lowering of the age at which the old age pension is paid so that it would be payable to all at the age of 60. He couples with that the very commendable suggestion that where the breadwinner is on pension the spouse should also receive the pension, even if that spouse has not yet reached the required age. In the second part of the motion the suggestion is made that the level of the pension should be sufficient to enable people to live as decently as is possible in this country.
I suspect that when we hear from the government side of the House in this debate there will be some who will give their support to this motion, their support to moving in the direction suggested by it, but I have no doubt that we will also be given a history of old age pensions. We will be told of the many improvements that have been made since 1926 when the first Old Age Pension Act was enacted. If one compares the original Old Age Pension Act with the present situation, there is no doubt in the world that a tremendous improvement has been made. That first act provided for $20 a month payable only at the age of 70, with a means test so rigorous that very few people were able to qualify for it. We now have a pension that is universal at age 65 to the extent of $80 per month for an individual, and we have the guaranteed income supplement which makes it possible for an individual without means to get an additional $55 for a total of $135 a month. It also makes it possible for a married couple without means to receive a total pension of $255 a month. A number of other improvements have been made, and I have no hesitation in welcoming the fact that we have come a long way since 1926 and 1927.

speechtext:
No, but it was in
this century, the early part of it.
I have no hesitation in saying that the improvements are welcome. But, Mr. Speaker, let us not get carried away with what we have done when, by comparison with what is needed, we are so far behind. If one compares the amount of the pension today with the total wealth we are producing in Canada, with the affluence many people enjoy, we just are not doing enough. We leave the old people in a position where they are entitled to say they are forgotten by the government and by Parliament. This notion that we can rest on our laurels because we passed an amendment to the Old Age Security Act in this session is not good enough for the Parliament of Canada.
October 21, 1971

The first proposal in this motion is one that we have to take seriously, namely, the lowering of the eligible age. I was interested in the very significant remarks made by the hon. member who preceded me, concerning the difference between chronological age and actual age. He has suggested ideas that should be given very serious consideration. However, what we have before us is a proposal that the eligible age be reduced from 65 to 60. I know that when this suggestion is made during the question period, there are some around who gasp and tell us how much it will cost. But we seem to find it possible to dig up $80 million for this, $90 million for that, and $1 billion for something else, and I think that if we were really aware of the importance of this problem we would find the money.
The point I should like to make is that we have to get away from the idea that an old age pension is merely something one gets when he is old and decrepit. We are in a society that is not finding it possible to provide full employment. This worries us. But it is also a fact of our age that we are moving into a time when there may be a lot less employment, a lot less actual physical work that has to be done. I hope the day will come in the lifetime of those of us here when great numbers of our people just will not be required to do physical work, or work in the actual production of goods and services, but will be free to enjoy life in various kinds of pursuits, and that society will make it possible for them to do so.
Instead of waiting until this type of life is forced on us, instead of bungling into it, why do we not decide now that age 60 is a good age for people to be permitted to leave the labour market. If one is forced to wait until 70, or even 65, in many cases one is not able to make the necessary adjustments or necessary shifts. But if we can say to people that they can retire from physical, manual or other labour at 60, and follow other pursuits, there is a chance for them to make that shift into the later part of life which, after all, is the best of all, for which the first is made-if my poetry isn't too mixed up.
Instead of thinking of pensions as a form of charity, of welfare, of something given to people because they are old and decrepit, there should be a firm decision on a time when we say, "You have done your share of the kind of drudgery that work demands. It is time for you to enjoy a guaranteed annual income. You have reached that age, now go out and show what you can do as human beings."
I suggest that we could think in terms of phasing into this situation. I suggest two ways, in case some are scandalized by the amount of money this would cost to do it all at once. When we reduced the eligible age from 70 to 65 years we faced this problem. Some people thought it would be too much to do it all at once, so we did it year by year, from 70 to 69, from 69 to 68, 68 to 67, 67 to 66, and finally from 66 to 65. We can do the same now. We can start next year to make it 64, the year after that 63, and so on until we get down to 60. This is something that will have to be considered.
Another way we could make this kind of transition is suggested to us in the way we treat the benefits under the Canada Pension Plan. We now provide that a person at age 70 gets the full benefits under the Canada Pension Plan to which he is entitled because of his contributions,
Old Age Security Pensions
no matter what he is doing, whether he is working or not, or has other income. Between 65 and 70, we permit persons to draw the benefits they have earned under the Canada Pension Plan on one condition only, namely, that they leave the labour market, that they do not have income from employment. It is no barrier to their full Canada Pension Plan benefits that persons may have income from investments and other sources. The only requirement is that they leave the labour market.
That might be a way for us to get started on the payment of old age pensions at age 60, simply by saying to people that it is optional-"if you leave the labour market you can get the full amount without regard to a means test, or other sources of income that you may have." Just as I have pleaded in this House over several decades for the various other improvements we have had to make in pensions, I think this question has to be taken seriously. That is why I commend my hon. friend from Roberval for placing it before us today.
Sometimes my hon. friends to my left are characterized as having strange ideas. It is also said that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) has some strange ideas, but he has been able to sell some of his strange ideas. I wish him luck with others. But the point of the matter is that strange or not, I think this is a serious proposition that society will have to face. I urge that this House today discuss it seriously, and try its best to make it known to the government that the issue of what we are doing about old age pensions is not over just because we passed an amending bill last December.
Part of the motion that is before us, part of the first sentence as it were, relates to the desirability of the pension being available to the spouse where that spouse is under the pension age if the breadwinner is on the pension. I hope that this, too, will be given serious consideration. I hope that we will not go through the routine that we usually go through when this comes up, that it is possible for some old codger to marry a young girl and then have her on the pension when she is 35, or even less. This could be taken care of by a simple regulation that the difference must be not more than five years, or that the couple must have been married for a certain number of years, or there could be the possibility of an employment test. I hope the House sees clearly that I do not under any circumstances suggest a means test. Ever since I came into this House the idea of a means test has been an anathema to me. I think there are other things in the labour market that are reasonable tests that could be applied. Let us not have the kind of nonsense that we sometimes have when this suggestion is made. It is a sound suggestion, and I think it should receive the attention and consideration of the House.
I have dealt thus far with what I regard as the first part of the motion, the first half, namely, the half that has to do with the lowering of the eligible age. As I say, I think that is the new thing that is before us in this motion. I do not mean that the suggestion is new because it has been made by some of us a good many times, but this is one of the few times that it has been before us as a motion, and I stress the seriousness and importance of it.
As I have already said there are times when people assert, and it has been asserted today, that one way to

October 21, 1971
Old Age Security Pensions
provide jobs for younger people is to get some of the older people out of the labour market. That may be oversimplifying it a bit, although there may be validity to that suggestion. But as I tried to say earlier this should be looked at in the context of the kind of over-all change which is taking place in society. I am as sure as I am that I am standing here that in the year 2,000 work will not have the important place in life that it has today. There will be millions of our people who will live for something else. Why don't we start now, deliberately choosing those groups of people who should not have to be in the labour market. I know of no better group to choose than our older people.
My friend from Simcoe North looked across the way a minute ago and, as a doctor, saw all sorts of medical conditions that he could attend to if he had time. I think one of the sad things about our retirement policy is that we have this tradition that you can work until you cannot do anything more, and then you are put out to pasture until you die. Why not accept the proposition that it is good at a reasonable time of life to retire from what one has been doing and to start over again? Now don't let anyone throw that at me-I have been here so long there is no other place for me to go. I intend to stay here arguing for this kind of thing and it may be of benefit to some of my friends across the way. There is my friend, the hon. member for Essex (Mr. Whelan). He has done a good job here and one thing I know, he will not be going to the other place. However, it might be a good idea if he were retired early so that he could make a contribution in some other way of life. And there are others across the way who might do the same thing.
I must not get sidetracked, Mr. Speaker, even if I am doing it myself because I want to say something about the second part of the motion. In fact, I want to move an amendment to it. I have shown my amendment to some of my friends to my left and have indicated to them that although it seeks to change a part of their wording, it is a friendly amendment that seeks to underline a certain aspect of this motion. The second part of the motion reads:
Any pension so awarded should be such as to enable anyone to live as decently as the physical, material and human resources of Canada would allow.
I agree. I just want to make the point and to underline it, that this means there must be a substantial increase in the amount of the pension now being paid. People cannot live and meet those conditions on $80 a month or $160 a month for man and wife. As for the people who qualify for $135 a month single or $255 a month married, they qualify only because they have practically nothing else. I think the circumstances that we have had since the guaranteed income supplement was brought in, and since these higher figures were set, prove the unfairness of a pension that has a means test attached to any portion of it.
While I think that we have been right on this side of the House over the years, and that the government was right when it accepted the principle of paying the pension universally, I think what we should now be doing is getting back to that principle and paying a pension of at least $150 across the board without any means test whatsoever.
(Mr. Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre).]
We can take care of the few wealthy people in the old age pension group by means of the income tax. That income tax is going to take care of all kinds of things if the bill ever gets through! The fact of the matter is that statistics prove that my hon. friend from Simcoe North was right. The number of wealthy people in the older age brackets is very low. Most are in need of every dollar they can get. Then, there is the whole problem of inflation which wipes out any increase. I think the minimum amount needed now is $150 a month across the board. To put it in precise terms, I think that is what my friend is asking for when he uses that rhetorical phrase that "any pension so awarded should be such as to enable anyone" to do such and such.
I have already got a motion on the order paper, Mr. Speaker, calling for pensions to be $150 a month, so I am afraid if I move that one at this point it might be looked upon by the Chair as repeating an argument taking place in another debate and therefore out of order. However, I think if I put my words in general terms they will meet the requirements of the rules, and therefore I want to propose that the amount paid as old age security should be substantially increased and by "substantially" I mean that it should be not less than $150 a month and that it should be' payable across the board.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I should like to move an amendment to the motion now before the House. I do so seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) and my motion is as follows:
That the motion be amended by deleting therefrom the words "Any pension so awarded should be such as", and by substituting therefor the words: "The amount of the pension now provided as old age security should be increased substantially".
If my motion were accepted, the total motion as amended would then read:
This House regrets that the government has not deemed advisable to provide old age security pensions to persons between the ages of 60 and 65, or to the wife of a retired person, whatever the age. The amount of the pension now provided as old age security should be increased substantially to enable anyone to live as decently as the physical, material and human resources of Canada would allow.
It was a good motion that the hon. member for Roberval brought in. I think it is a better motion with the change I have made in it, and I hope the House, throughout the day, will indicate its support.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ELIGIBILITY TO OLD AGE SECURITY OF PERSONS 60 TO 65 YEARS OF AGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure that I have supported the motion moved by my colleague the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier), requesting the government to provide the old age security pension all those between 60 and 65, as well as to the wife, whatever her age may be.
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Parliament, in 1965, passed a law to bring the pension age down from 70 to 65 and today anyone aged 65 is entitled to this pension. Until 1967, the pension was established at $75 per month, but since 1968, the amount can be increased according to the rise in the cost of living, and it now stands at $79.58. And in January 1971, the maximum was increased by 42 cents, so as to become a monthly payment of $80.
Mr. Speaker, this government is presently incapable of finding jobs for the unemployed. During periods of unemployment, as is now the case, public opinion calls for a lower retirement age, so that more old people can withdraw from the labour market thus making room for younger people.
Mr. Speaker, legislation passed in Denmark in 1891 set at 60 the retirement age, but it was amended in 1932 to raise it to 65. Even if this was a backward step with respect to the 1891 legislation, it provided some compensation. For example, under special circumstances, local authorities could, with the approval of the responsible minister, grant the pensions at 60.
Mr. Speaker, the legislation passed in New Zealand in 1898 provided a pension to the citizens of 65 and over. An amendment passed in 1911 reduced it to 60 and to 55 for women, when the applicants had two young dependents of 15 or under. Another amendment passed in 1913 granted a retirement pension to all women of 60 or over.
Mr. Speaker, the law that was passed in Australia in 1908 granted old age pension to men and women of 65 and over. That minimum age was lowered to 60 in 1910.
In China a few years ago, older people starved to death in the streets. Nowadays, people of 50 and 55 in that immense and over-populated country receive the old age pension. Canada cannot be left behind in this vital question of age.
Mr. Speaker, the government seems to think we are asking for something impossible, yet considering Canada's physical possibilities to produce, we all agree that we could produce for a population twice the size of ours. Indeed, we are 50 years behind as concerns the application of this old age pension to cover people at 60. Mr. Speaker, Canada must face stronger and stronger foreign competition. It should endeavour to increase its manufacturing efficiency. In other words, it should increase productivity. Now, account should be taken of the development of new techniques older workers, 60 years and over, find it hard to get used to.
According to a study conducted by the Economy and Research Branch of the federal Department of Labor in 1960 and published under the title "Age and Efficiency", maximum efficiency obtains at 55 and tends to decrease thereafter.
Old Age Security Pensions
Mr. Speaker, in my constituency, there are many cases of married couples where the husband receives a pension, whereas the wife, being younger, has to be satisfied with a small welfare allowance. This is an unfortunate situation. After having brought up a fairly large family, one should not have to live under inhuman conditions, although that is often the case. The reason is that there is no money to buy the necessities of life while we are living in affluence and that department stores in all our cities are bursting with those goods which could make our families so happy.
During summer adjournment, I convassed from door to door in my riding to make on the spot enquiries. I believe that if the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his cabinet members, in charge of the laws on old age pensions, could do the same they would see the deplorable living conditions of many aged couples and this would prompt the cabinet to make a faster decision. But the Prime Minister and his cabinet are satisfied with travelling around the world to try and sell our products of which many Canadian families are in great need but the almighty dollar does not work for people's needs but for those who control our economic blood; even more important, the election fund must be replenished.

In a pre-election speech in the fall of 1935, the late Right Hon. Mackenzie King declared at the opening of the electoral campaign and I quote:
Until the control of currency and credit is restored to Parliament and recognized as its most evident and most sacred responsibility all talk of democracy is idle and futile. A truly national bank, properly constituted, should control the issue of money in terms of public need.
The flow of money must be in relation with the domestic, social and industrial needs of the Canadian people.
I think this was a very true statement, but just like all the other Liberal promises, it was never respected. It was just another trap to get voters to vote for the party. Since 1930, Canadian people have been asking questions about our Canadian monetary policy. Canadians wonder why we have so much in time of war and so little in time of peace, so much for underdeveloped countries and so little to develop Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I would ask the government to set up a royal commission to find out if we have enough products to pay our older people a pension as soon as they reach age 60.
Mr. Speaker, we make all sorts of studies but it would be important to know if our country has enough products to pay our older people a pension as soon as they reach age 60. I think our country has the necessary products to help those people.
There is a particular case I would like to single out. Two older people from Malartic came to see me, one is 71 and the other 74 years old. These two persons have a joint bank account where each deposited $1,000. The father was telling me, we do not want to touch it, it is for our burial. At the end of each year, the bank files a report indicating that they received a small amount of interest. So the federal government takes away part of the interest they receive. Instead of getting the maximum $255 a

October 21, 1971
8898	_________________________________
Old Age Security Pensions
month, they get roughly $248 a month because they each have $1,000.
I think that this should not be tolerated in a country as rich as Canada.
I have recently seen a family in Val d'Or, where the father is 74 years of age and the mother 57, and they have a totally incapacitated son of 27 and an ailing daughter. The father draws the $135 maximum pension, the son $75, the daughter $80 and the mother nought. This is a situation which happens in Canada. Four people must live on $290. How can they manage?
The hon. member for Roberval stated a few moments ago that an employee is forced to leave his job at the age of 65 and is eligible to only three weeks of unemployment insurance benefits and the maximum he can receive is $80 a month, a year earlier, if the same person aged 65 who left his work by reason of his age was available for work, he could draw unemployment insurance benefits together with his monthly pension of $80, $79 or $58. Here is a person who could live with a measure of decency for at least a year. But the investigating officers realized that there was some money to be gotten out of these families and this is how people are penalized.
Mr. Speaker, I will say no more on the subject, but ask once again the government to fall in with the request that old age security pensions be provided to persons aged 60. The government of Canada would be well deserving of the ratefulness of the Canadian people by instituting forthwith an integral scheme whereby pensions would be provided to persons aged 60 and to the wife of a retired person, whatever the age.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ELIGIBILITY TO OLD AGE SECURITY OF PERSONS 60 TO 65 YEARS OF AGE
speechtext:
It was good of the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) to put forward his motion today. It gives us an opportunity to pause for a while and give some thought to the question of the retirement in dignity of people in Canada, considering the fact that they have contributed to our society in a productive manner all their lives and that they therefore have the right to a pension which will permit them to live in dignity.
The thrust of the motion put forward by the hon. member for Roberval is concentrated around the approach that is made available by means of the old age security pension. This is the measure he has emphasized and which he would like to expand further to include people whose age is 60 and over. In discussing the manner whereby he would finance this proposal, if I am interpreting him correctly, he said the necessary funds could be found by reducing or eliminating payments to recipients of unemployment insurance benefits, by reducing or eliminating payments to trainees under manpower auspices and by reducing the number of people employed as civil servants to administer certain programs.
It seems to me this is an awkward way in which to go about providing benefits of the kind envisaged. It is perhaps outdated in the sense that it looks only at one social benefit measure, without taking into account that with every year that goes by we are closer to the fruition of 
another social insurance measure of great importance to Canadians, namely, the Canada Pension Plan which was introduced in the House in 1965, I believe. It seems to me that if we are to achieve the objective outlined by the hon. member, namely, the extension of pension benefits to other segments in our community, we could do so more effectively and more generously by paying attention to the Canada Pension Plan and to some of the provisions it contains. There are provisions in the plan which would permit us to achieve this objective earlier if it were possible to accelerate the year in which full rates are to be made available, namely, to introduce full rates earlier than 1976. This would only be possible, of course, if Canadians were willing to increase their premiums to this contributory plan thus enabling the year of maturity of the plan itself to be advanced.
Another step which might go a long way to meeting the hon. member's objective would be to raise the ceiling on pensioners' earnings. This would increase the number of people who would benefit. Rather than by means of increasing taxes in a manner the hon. member for Roberval did not really specifically outline, except by indicating that certain useful programs which exist at present should be eliminated, the Canada Pension Plan offers a vehicle of self-imposed taxation and contributions which makes much more sense.
This discussion also provides us with an opportunity to consider a question which has been raised, I suppose, by other hon. members on other occasions, that is to say, whether we should continue to regard the age of 60 as the age at which people have reached a stage in life at which they should retire from the productive labour force. It seems to me there is another way to go about it. We could revise this concept of a fixed retirement age and substitute a flexible retirement clause. This would tie in with some of the ideas expressed by the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard) when he spoke of two different ages, the calendar age and the physical age. Rather than be tied down by a calendar age, it seems to me we could achieve greater social benefits by thinking in terms of a flexible retirement age. This would permit an individual to retire from active productive life at the age at which he or she wished to do so. In some cases it would be well above the age of 65; in others it might be well below.
It is this concept which might be considered by the minister and the officials in charge of the Canada Pension Plan when embarking upon consultations with provincial governments as they are scheduled to do in years to come. It makes sense that a flexible retirement clause should be part and parcel of a social security scheme. Canadians would then be able to retire when they wished to do so and become entitled to certain benefits on their own terms, rather than in accordance with a rigid concept which is difficult to apply in day to day life. May I add that this concept is not only not new but has already been incorporated in the legislation of some other countries. For instance, I understand that the pension plan operated by the Federal Republic of Germany, as recently amended, introduces this same concept of flexible retirement. That country has also introduced at the same time the one-year credit concept for mothers who have to withdraw from the labour force. This kind of pioneering in the
October 21, 1971

field of social measures would, if adapted to our own needs, considerably benefit pensioners in Canada.
In examining the approach developed by the hon. member for Roberval, who suggested we could achieve a similar objective if not a better one, through the Canada pension plan, I would suggest that in doing so it would be desirable to co-ordinate social measures with other federal programs. For instance, it would be desirable to coordinate the Canada Pension Plan with the unemployment insurance plan, thereby offering flexible retirement when workers decide to withdraw. Perhaps we might even introduce incentives to withdraw that are even more attractive than the present incentives.
Let me give the House an example, Mr. Speaker. If I recall correctly, under the unemployment insurance legislation approved by this House, if a person aged 65 or over decides to retire and take a pension under the Canada Pension Plan he receives a lump sum payment amounting to three weeks' salary. However, should this person decide not to retire but to continue to make himself available for employment-this person is assumed to be unemployed- he can continue to receive unemployment insurance benefits for almost one year. There is a considerable difference in the amount that this person will receive, depending upon which approach he decides to adopt. It seems to me that the incentive offered by the lump sum payment is much less than the benefit that this person would receive were he to decide to remain available for employment. I just give this example to underline the importance, as already indicated by others before me, of co-ordinating the Canada Pension Plan with other social measures, such as unemployment insurance, in order to offer the maximum benefit.
Before concluding may I make reference to one aspect of our old age security legislation which has not been debated today. I refer to immigrants who wish to retire in their native land. Under the present provisions, an immigrant is permitted to receive his old age security pension should he decide to return to his native land only when he has been resident in Canada for 25 years. This opportunity has been taken by some who felt that, for health or sentimental reasons, it was necessary for them to retire in their country of origin. This measure has also been made use of by others who felt that the sum made available by old age security would go further in their native land where the cost of living was lower. In recent years a number of representations have been made to the government by different groups who have stressed the desirability of reducing the number of years residence from 25 so as to permit individuals, who perhaps have reached the age of retirement but have been resident in Canada only 20 or 23 years, to retire to their native country.
It seems to me this is a matter about which arguments can be made either way. At the same time, I should like to take this opportunity of drawing this question to the attention of the minister. I urge him to consider requests made over the years to reduce the residence requirement. If this is possible I am sure it would be most appreciated by those who wish to take advantage of such a provision.
Old Age Security Pensions

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take this opportunity to say a few words on behalf of the older citizens of Canada. No section of the Canadian populace has suffered more under this government's outmoded approach to the economy than our senior citizens. No section of our populace has suffered more from the deliberate and cold-blooded effort by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to fight inflation by creating unemployment.
It has often been said that the war against inflation is fought on the backs of the poor. I know that our senior citizens will agree with that statement. After working all their lives to try to accumulate enough to live on in decency for the balance of their lives, these people now find their pensions and savings chopped away by inflation. They are denied any satisfactory measure of relief by a government which can find hundreds of millions of dollars to squander on unnecessary projects, but little if any assistance to offer the old age pensioners.
I would be the first to agree that the conditions for the old age pensioner have improved over the last 20 or 30 years. May I also say formally that we cannot rest on our laurels. Much needs to be done for these people. If I need to support that statement, I can do no better than refer to statements made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro). I was interested to note, in glancing through some remarks that the minister made at the federal-provincial conference of welfare ministers last January, that he recognized that unemployment was higher than ever before in this country, that many, many more human lives were in jeopardy in this country and that those people were depending on social welfare assistance. After referring to the various programs the government has in mind, he went on to say:
The main thrust of the federal policy in this field-
Meaning the whole field of social assistance.
-for the future will be:
1.	to develop the guaranteed income technique as a major anti-poverty policy;
2.	to reduce emphasis on universal programs like old age security and family allowances and place greater emphasis on selective programs providing income-related benefits under Guaranteed Income Supplement and Family Income Security Plan;
Today, we are concerned only about the guaranteed income supplement part of the statement. I think the minister's remarks are enlightening and show that he recognizes that much more must be done for our older citizens if they are to live in any sort of decent retirement.
The minister also discussed the question of assistance as a right, something that has been argued over the years. I was pleased to see his statement to the effect that governments must now recognize that the provision of this type of assistance constitutes a right and that this is what the government intends to provide. That, to me, demonstrates clearly the wisdom of a motion of the type we are considering. The necessity is there. In the few minutes I shall talk, I want to point out some of the weaknesses of the present system and make suggestions for betterment.

October 21, 1971
Old Age Security Pensions
Canada's senior citizens make up a large proportion of those affected by poverty. They had high hopes as a result of the white paper on income security; yet, since being introduced in November, 1970, the white paper has been subject to a heavy barrage of criticism from all sectors of Canadian society. Its critics include social welfare workers, journalists and economists. They come from all sections of the population. The white paper, prepared under the direction of Deputy Minister Joseph Willard, took two years to research. Canadians expected the white paper to include the announcement of a broad, new social policy for this country. Yet, when the programs were announced, it became evident that the Minister of National Health and Welfare had lost in his fight for a comprehensive social program. After 18 months of cabinet in-fighting, a very feeble document was introduced on November 30, 1970.
The proposals in this document advocated three main changes. The first related to family allowances; the second, to old age payments and the income supplement, and the third, to the Canada Pension Plan. At this time, in this debate, I am concerned only about proposals or suggestions relating to old age pensions and the guaranteed income supplement. My criticism of these proposals and of our present system falls under two headings: the first is the old age security plan itself and the second, the guaranteed income supplement.
It is amazing that the criticism of these two plans has been so widespread and uniform, although the critics have come from a diversity of backgrounds. One of the things that has surprised critics is the speed with which the government enacted into law those parts of the white paper dealing with old age security and the guaranteed income supplement. The speed with which they brought those programs in was unusual for this government. Up to the present, the government has brought out white papers, with the avowed intention of giving people lots of time to study them, make proposals and suggestions and, hopefully, bring about improvements. In this instance, no opportunity was given to anyone to study the proposals in the white paper. There was no opportunity for organizations and people to suggest amendments.
The old age security and guaranteed income supplement benefits, even with the increases provided in the spring of this year, still fall short of the minimum required for a satisfactory standard of living for the aged. Few of our old people will be removed from poverty as a result of the increase. Furthermore, as critics have pointed out, income tax at present rates reduces the payments in many instances, particularly for single people; and, even if the proposals for tax amendments are adopted, single people and some couples under 70 will suffer an income reduction through taxation.
There has also been a criticism of the fact that the universal program, that is, the old age security plan, was not "beefed up". Why was there such a meagre increase? It was about 40 cents a month, as I recall. Here is a payment that is given to all people who are over 65. If you want to see how great the need is for an increased basic amount, you only need to look at the figures. About 50 per cent of our people on old age security are receiving the guaranteed income supplement; more than half of these people get the full supplement. Clearly, the need is there.

These older people just do not have the necessary income on which to exist.
The flat rate of $80 for old age security, even with the cost of living escalation of 2 per cent for the guaranteed income supplement, is not realistic when we consider that the cost of living index has been rising by 4 or 5 per cent annually. If the past performance of the economy is repeated in the future, and there is nothing to indicate that the increase in the cost of living index will be lower- indications are that it will continue to rise by at least 4 or 5 per cent-the result will be that in 25 years today's $80 will buy something less than $40 worth of goods and services. At the end of 50 years it will not buy anything. The sad part is that pensioners are at the mercy of the system. They have no way of bargaining for wage increases, as everybody else does. This action by the government is even more unfair when we realize that old age pensions were directly paid for, in part, by the pensioners themselves. They have contribute dto thes epensions through automatic tax deductions and have taken into considerations pension payments in figuring out how much will be available to them at retirement.
Another serious criticism of the present legislation is that old age pensioners are still taxed on income they earn on top of the government allowances. For each $2 of income in excess of the pension, $1 will be taken away in taxes. There are many ways in which this practice of deducting $1 for every $2 can be shown to be both undesirable and unfair. For example, many older people have substantial savings but low income and are receiving the supplement. Other people with no savings but with incomes only slightly above the present maximum receive nothing. When the working corps becomes the retired corps and eligible for the guaranteed income supplement, they find their Canada Pension Plan payments are cut because they are taxable. Can we blame them if they feel they are effectively paying a 50 per cent rate of income tax on their Canada Pension Plan pensions, even though their retirement income may be below the poverty level? As a result of this, many old age pensioners, even though they are healthy and well enough to take outside jobs, feel it would not be to their advantage to accept these jobs. Such a penalty is not consistent with the allegations in the white paper of last year that the major reason for not adopting the guaranteed annual income centres around a need to develop a suitable work incentive for such a plan.
There are many glaring examples. I have received many letters as I am sure have other members. One letter I received deals with the case of an old age pensioner who is not able to work and whose wife is under the age at which she would be eligible for the pension. She has to go to work, probably to help pay the drug bills for the pensioner. When she goes to work she immediately finds the guaranteed income supplement is reduced or taken away entirely. This is a ridiculous situation and is one which is not fair to the older citizen. Every time we suggest changes, the government asks where the money is to come from. These are changes perhaps of a minor nature, but they are of very great importance to the pensioners who are involved. I do not think the cost in dollars would be so
October 21, 1971

great that it should be met with a reply to the effect that this is fine but where is the money to come from.
There are many other anomalies and hardships which our present system works on the old age pensioner. For example, even at a time when the government is trying to encourage savings and to encourage people to take part in the financing of the country, the older person is discouraged from purchasing government bonds because the interest on those bonds would be considered income so his guaranteed income supplement could be lowered. Because of these laws people are encouraged to remain in dwellings which probably are too big for their requirements. Because the dwelling is paid for, these people feel they have no alternative but to live there rather than rent smaller premises which would be more suitable for them in their old age.
These are some of the criticisms I wanted to bring forward in this short space of time. As I remarked, they are not of such a far reaching nature as to represent a great drain on the treasury and yet are very important to these people involved. I have been very encouraged by the fact that the minister has recognized the needs of our older people. The quotation from his remarks to which I referred at the start of my speech indicates that the minister is aware of these problems. The question now is not whether these people should be helped, but how. I am encouraged by the fact that the minister has indicated his willingness to accept suggestions. I hope he will accept some of the suggestions made here today and push ahead with plans to develop a rational and reasonable social assistance welfare services program.
