speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I first want to express my appreciation and that of the hon. members of my party and of all parties in the House for the good service rendered by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) in moving this motion, because he has drawn the attention of the whole House to the very serious problems of all the older people in our great country. I am sure that we are all happy that he has moved this motion this afternoon, and I want to congratulate him.

As the first spokesman for our party, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has said we heartily support the motion introduced by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier). Our only suggestion in the form of an amendment has been that we would like to see something a little more definite. We would like to see the amount of the benefit now provided as old age security substantially increased. I believe our concern in introducing this amendment arises from the fact that, as outlined by the hon. member who spoke on behalf of the government party, there are many other things which could be introduced to help the elderly people who need income at the present time. He expounded at great length on the various alternative ways and means by which this could be done. Yet, at no stage do I believe he said this motion was not a good one, except of course he implied it would be a very expensive one, at least in respect of those people who would be pensionable at 60 years of age.
Old Age Security Pensions
The fact is that the elderly people in this country suffer more and more as the months and years go by. They suffer for a great variety of reasons. I do not think little bits of patches here and there and yonder will be sufficient to help in this case. Obviously, as the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard) said, there are pockets of injustice here and there which need eliminating. The elimination of pockets of injustice, however, will not deal with the very great difficulty which exists now in respect of the older people. The overriding problem of the older people is that they do not have enough money on which to live. Their pensions are not adequate. As time goes on and as living costs increase in a whole variety of directions, and as their little bits of revenue decrease, the problem becomes more and more acute. No amount of patching up in respect of the abuses and injustices will solve the main problem of how to get enough income into the hands of the thousands and thousands of elderly people which they require in order to live decently.
I wish to point out to members opposite, particularly the hon. member who just spoke, that there is nothing in this motion or in the minds of any of us on this side, that would prevent a flexible approach in respect of the old age pension. That does not mean a means test. We have been told about the situation in Germany and I would add Britain and other places where the application of the old age pension is flexible depending on the age, vitality and will of the person to continue working. We in no way would interfere with that. I think it would be a very bad thing indeed to lower the boom on people at the age of 60 by simply saying that everybody who reaches the age of 60 must stop gainful employment. There are a great many people who, having gone beyond the age of 60, still have sufficient strength, vitality, intelligence and devotion to make great contributions.
.00 p.m.)
On looking at this motion, one sees that it is very simple and logical. It suggests the lowering of the pensionable age to the age of 60 for all people. In my view, it does one very good thing right away. It brings back the principle of universality to a place from which it should never have been taken. I have never been able to understand why the government cannot bear to use the income tax as a means of getting back from people who do not need it the full amount of the old age pension that is paid to them, and a great deal more, in order to help the other people. Why is it not simpler, easier and more fair to make the pension available as a matter of right, and then use the income tax in a fair way to get the pension back from all those who do not need it?
One thing I want to point out is that ever since the inception of the old age pension it has never been set at a level which covered the actual cost of living. Since no attempt has ever been made to find out what it actually costs to live, pensions have not been based on it. As a matter of fact, a few years ago the Senate Committee on Aging pointed out clearly that one of the things that was required in connection with the old age pension was the establishment of a technically competent body to study the income needs of older people and the development of a socially acceptable minimum budget for single persons as well as for couples, which would be adjusted automati-

October 21, 1971
Old Age Security Pensions
cally each year on the basis of a suitable index of consumer spending or of earnings. This minimum budget would be reviewed every five years to reflect changes in the relative circumstances of the working population and of the retired population.
So far as I am aware, and I know what has happened with old age pensions since the beginning, there has never been any competent body told to find out what it costs older people to live so that pensions could be set in accordance with it. Pension increases have always been set on the basis of the least possible amount that could be given which would keep the government viable politically. In my view, this is not the way to approach this matter. We should take to heart the recommendation of the Senate Committee on Aging, and before anything else is done to old age pensions we should find out right now how much it costs pensioners to live and then set the pensions at that level, with an escalator clause. We should also ensure there are sufficiently frequent reviews to keep the old age pensions moving in accordance with the cost of living.
Old age pensioners should no longer be divided into well-off and less well-off pensioners, since none of them is well off. There should not be such discrimination on the basis of whether one group has a few dollars available for their emergency needs or for their funerals. They should be considered as one group of retired people who should have a fair pension and who should be able to enjoy it. If some of them are able to earn more money after they retire, so what? Surely, they should be allowed to earn that money without a means test, and the computer can find out how much should be returned in income tax at the end of the year.
This motion has one or two very interesting features in it. One of them is that when a pension is paid at the age of 60 instead of 65, the spouse of the pensioner should also receive a pension, regardless of her age. We have heard people say that this is an incentive for elderly men to marry very young girls so that they will get a double income in the form of pension. I remember some years ago when a former cabinet minister, whom I shall not name because he is still living although he is no longer in the cabinet, during a discussion of the medicare scheme said he was very much opposed to it because he thought this would be an incentive for people to throw themselves under trains or to have industrial accidents in order to qualify for benefits. This is the same sort of logic as is being used in this argument. I believe that this aspect of the motion takes account of a very real need. In most cases the wife of the pensioner is only a few years younger. When the husband retires, his pay cheque is cut off and they both have to live on his pension. I am in sympathy with the idea of a pension being paid to the spouse of a pensioner who has no other source of income. If she is in the labour force, there may be regulations to provide for that contingency, but the intent of this resolution is to ensure that the spouse has enough on which to live.
There is another group about which I would like to say a few words. I am referring to women who, with all respect to what was said on the other side of the House about what could be done under the Canada Pension Plan to help elderly people, are not covered by the Canada

Pension Plan so far as I can see. These are women who are spinsters or those who were casually employed when they were young, or those whose husbands have died, or those who have separated. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) said that most women over the age of 40 cannot get a job these days. I do not consider baby sitting and housework as being a job. This just provides pin money. Today, any woman over the age of 40, unless she is really lucky, cannot get a job. There is a great gap between the age of 40 and the age of 65. I have received many letters from women in this group who have no income and have to rely on social assistance. It tears them apart to have to go on social assistance for all those years, with the resultant lowering of living standards as well as the indignity.
I would like to make a special plea for those women and emphasize the need to lower the pensionable age. If we can lower it to the age of 60, it will help to look after women who cannot earn a living before they reach the present pensionable age of 65. This will cover many widows and women who are separated or divorced. It will not cover all of them, but it would help. I would like to urge that we consider them. There are many women who are alone and without a job and who have to rely on social assistance. They do not qualify for low income housing for families and they do not qualify for housing for older people. They are at the mercy of the landlords. They are in a bad way, indeed.
In supporting this motion we should take account of the fact that today elderly people are in a very different situation from that which existed several generations ago. The reason young people today regard old age with such unqualified horror is that for so many people old age is becoming a time of penury and poverty. The younger people think it is pretty awful to have your teeth falling out, your hair falling out, your insides being taken because of various diseases, with all kinds of disabilities setting in, and being regarded as a supernumerary. To them, it is just too much. They consider that there is nothing worse than old age.
Old age used to be considered more dignified because then there was the family circle. There was housing for that family circle. There was attention, and there was affection within the family circle. Elderly people had a part to play. But today, people have moved into the big cities, into tiny little houses where there is no room for elderly people. More and more elderly people have nothing to live on except what the government gives them in the form of pensions and relief. Today, they are in a very bad way. Today, they do not even have a true old age pension. It was pointed out by one hon. member to my left that what they have is part pension and part social welfare. This is true for those who are not fortunate enough to qualify for the $80, and those who do not consider themselves fortunate because no matter how the cost of living goes up their pension does not go up.
Elderly people's needs for health care and drugs are not covered. The hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard), who is a member of the medical profession, pointed out that last year the drug bill in Canada was $271 million. This is not covered by medicare. Old people who
October 21, 1971

are not on social assistance have to go short of food and other necessities in order to try and get the drugs which are essential to treat the ailments associated with old age. Today elderly people are in a vastly different position from that which they used to occupy. An increasing number of them is dependent completely on what the community can do for them, through government services and through the pension. When we think of economizing the last place we should economize is the pensions for the elderly which would provide them with a decent living.
I urge that the House support the motion presented by the hon. member for Roberval. The eligible age should be reduced to 60 years, and there should be some flexibility provided to allow people to continue earning. There should be a substantial increase in old age pensions. We should determine the amount after finding out what it costs to live today. There should be an escalator provision in all pensions, and everybody should get the pension at age 60. Let us put our computers to work to determine the necessary amounts, to retrieve pension payments from millionaires, and make sure that those who arrive at age 60 have a chance to live out their days in a dignified, worth-while manner.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ELIGIBILITY OF PERSONS AGED 60 TO 65 FOR OLD AGE SECURITY PENSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to have this opportunity of speaking in favour of the motion moved by my colleague, the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier).
This motion, to my mind very important, deals with a problem that is getting more serious everyday, that of the people of 60 to 65.
We are now going through a very difficult period as far as employment is concerned. The latest reports on unemployment published by Statistics Canada and the Department of Manpower and Immigration on October 14, showed that 434,000 people were unemployed in Canada at the end of the week ending September 18 1971.
Statistics also indicated a marked increase in the number of unemployed in the 14 to 24 age group. The situation is certainly serious because the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) tabled supplementary estimates including many programs to create more jobs in the next months.
I am sorry to find that young people have a hard time finding employment; I think this should not be at the present time. These are our best workers, our best brains, and they are ready to participate in the economy of the country. In view of this situation, many people and groups now demand that the pension age be lowered to 60 years.
It is useless to try and find out what those who have reached 60 think when the matter of asking them to retire comes up. Some would be prepared to retire after 40 or 45 years of work, but the loss of their only income does not allow them to consider an early retirement at 60.
As to those who have reached that age, when they apply for a job, they are sometimes asked how old they are. After a cursory look, they are told there is nothing for them on account of their age.
Such an answer is disheartening for those who have worked hard all their lives but who are still willing to contribute to the economic life of the country through their work, while receiving at the same time a salary which would allow them as well as their family to live decently.
Things are even harder for families in which one or two children are still in school, and the father's is the only income. Then there are those men who are sick or exhausted, and just do not have the physical strength to compete with younger, fitter workers. The labour market has become increasingly demanding. Machines which have taken the place of man run at very high speed and demand more energy from the people who operate them, so that in many cases, when he reaches an advanced age, the same man cannot keep up with production requirements because of his physical condition.
I could quote many similar examples. The problem which affects all of us is this: the number of unemployed is increasing all the time. More and more young people join the labour force every year. People who have reached 60 find it increasingly difficult to remain on the labour market, for the reasons I have just mentioned. Are we going to leave them and their families without an income? I do not think this would be worthy of a country which calls itself wealthy and even claims that it is one of the

October 21, 1971
Old Age Security Pensions
richest in the world. We must quite urgently have a look at this and find a just solution for those people who certainly are entitled to a decent life after all the years they have served their families and their country.
To put the matter off is not a solution, Mr. Speaker. That would amount to ignoring the situation. That problem has been throughly investigated in several countries. A document published in 1932 by the International Labour Conference says that the minimum retirement age should not be beyond 65. As I said, that report was published in 1932. In Canada it took 35 years to take into account that recommendation of the International Labour Organization.
Indeed there may be different views according to economic needs. When there is unemployment, as it is the case today, public opinion wants the retirement age to be reduced so that more old people will quit the labour market to make way for young people who are entering that labour market. We must also stress the fact that the difficulty older people have in getting a job confirms that it is necessary to lower the retirement age.
That is what happened in Denmark in 1932 when labour unions requested that retirement age be brought down from 65 to 60, which was in fact done in 1937.
The same reactions prompted British unions to demand retirement at an earlier age and an increase in the age of compulsory school attendance, in order to reduce the number of people on the labour market.
In New Zealand, as early as 1898, retirement pensions were paid at age 65 and an amendment passed in 1911 brought this down to age 60.
In 1908, Australia passed a similar legislation for persons aged 65 and the minimum age was reduced to 60 in 1910.
In Canada, only in 1927 was legislation passed granting payment of a $20 a month pension to people aged 70 and over. Among the industrialized countries, we were one of the last to pass legislation providing a retirement pension and it is only two years ago that those who have reached age 65 have been entitled to draw this pension. We certainly don't hold the speed record when it comes to producing legislation to help the retired. Mind you, I don't intend to blame the various governments we have had since 1900, nor can one government take the credit for passing this legislation or for amending it during the last 15 years. The only ones I could address congratulations to for this law are the Canadian citizens who have agreed to support its costs.
At election time, there have been some mischievous people who took pleasure in intimidating those who were in receipt of a federal government retirement pension, by saying that if they did not support this or that candidate, they would lose their pension. Those who intimidated our retired people in this manner were dishonest. I say that if we are behind some countries as far as improving our pensions program is concerned, it is likely attributable to people of this caliber.
I would like to deal with another matter which surely deserves serious consideration, that is the excessive
number of social assistance programs, which duplicate one another. At the present time, I believe there is need in Canada to reconsider social programs in order to eliminate bureaucracy which is becoming more and more rampant. In some fields, programs seem to have expanded inordinately, considering the aid that the people can receive from them.
Some persons receive the old age pension, a small amount under the Quebec or the Canada Pension Plan and, sometimes, an allowance from the Department of Health, Family and Social Welfare. They receive money from three different sources and all this is not enough to enable them to live decently. This example shows that we are over administered. There is uneasiness and lack of coordination concerning the application of all assistance programs in Canada, whether at the federal, provincial or municipal level. All administrative levels demand exclusiveness and priority, without ever coming to an understanding. This is sheer pandemonium. And those who really need help must sometimes deal with several offices before managing to get a meagre allowance which barely keeps starvation away.
Those who pay for this fancy are, first, the people in need of assistance, second, "Bateeste" the taxpayer who, every week, sees the amount of his pay cheque decrease, whereas the deductions on his cheque stub keep on increasing, third, the employer who, at the end of every month, is never done with sending reports to various governments and this under the threat that if the reports do not reach the departments on a specified date, a surcharge will be levied. Employers have also become a cog in the bureaucratic system.
As a result there are a loss of time, a decrease in production and an increase in prices.
It is time to put an end to similar programs which are a waste of public funds. If we sincerely want to alleviate destitution and obtain a minimum of efficiency, the federal government must first-followed by the provincial governments-take the necessary steps to remove in certain cases that cumbersome and useless redtape and this as soon as possible, if we do not want to crush those who through their taxes contribute to the administration of the country.
In 1968, when it came into office, the government stated that it would use all possible means to attain the highest degree of efficiency and this at less cost. Where are the changes?
The Prime Minister himself dealt with the matter with so much assurance that even those who did not share his views really believed what he said and hoped for a change.
In that regard, I would like to quote the words of the Prime Minister himself, as reported in a commercial advertisement published by the Liberal Party of Canada in June 15, 1968 issue of the magazine La terre de chez nous, and I quote:
I believe in progress. I believe in evolution. I believe we have the duty of not trying to stick to everything from the past. I believe we must make experiments, risk solutions that are necessary if we want to enter tomorrow's world and not linger in yesterday's.
Canada offers many signs of bad wealth distribution. For instance, in the whole rural population, including fishermen, farm-

October 21, 1971

ers and forest workers, there are people who live in intolerable economic conditions. Now, that is unacceptable. But what is also unacceptable is that many politicians seem to consider this situation only as a secondary problem.
He who seeks to please everybody by lessening his positions or making a compromise with his convictions eventually ends up with neither position nor convictions. What one really believes he must say simply, clearly and without guile.
It was fine to establish priorities and to generate hope in the minds of the people; it was indeed necessary. After three years, nothing warrants that those objectives will be reached. I even wonder whether they are still pursued. I would rather think that all those programs have been shelved together with the other election promises.
Mr. Speaker, in all fairness for the have-not groups, the time has now come to work seriously, by brushing off all the impediments which build up an impassable barrier to the real wealth of this country, which is available has has been accumulated by men to meet the needs of one and all.
What prevents production from meeting consumption and reaching the population is that impassable barrier erected between production and distribution; it is too high indeed and to protect some private interests, no opening has been provided.
What is this obstacle in front of us? It is the financial system assisted by its best device bureaucracy.
Each time people request improvements, new structures which more and more difficult to reach, are created; when they can be reached, some extremely complicated regulations are made. Sometime, even public servants contradict each other and understand nothing.
In the meantime, people suffer, are deprived of necessities and the whole economy of the country is slowed down by that bureaucracy.
If democracy still exists, if it is not a topic discussed in living rooms only, if it is not an empty word, it is up to this government to eliminate the obstacles it has created. If the government is really sovereign and responsible to the people, it must and can take action, otherwise we will have to believe the Right Honourable Mackenzie King was right when he said in 1935, and I quote:
As soon as a nation gives up control of its credit, it matters little who makes the laws. As long as the control of money and credit are not given back to the government and recognized as its most important responsibility, one cannot speak of the sovereignty of parliament and democracy.
Mr. Gerry McGeer, former mayor of Vancouver, who sat in the House of Commons as member for the liberal party in 1935, speaking to an audience, stated as follows:
If the Canadian government could delegate to the banks through an act, the privilege of creating the credit of the nation, surely it could claim back, on behalf of the nation, the same privilege by introducing another legislation.
Mr. McGeer added, addressing the reporters who had asked him questions:
My answer is that the government could pass an act to regain control of its credit; that would be constitutional and it could be done simply by amending the bank act and the financial administration act.
Old Age Security Pensions
To my mind, as long as the government does not remove those artificial stumbling blocks, the nation will go from bad to worse. We must remove them.
It is time we had a single program to provide a guaranteed social income to all Canadians.
Since the beginning of my term of office in the House of Commons in 1968, I have received many letters from my constituents and even from other Canadians whose age vary between 60 and 65. They tell me that their physical condition does not allow them to work or that they are unemployed and they ask me to help them find a new job.
This is why a motion, which I support, was proposed by my colleague the member for Roberval.
Those who reach age 60 are demanding the passage of such legislation. A bill granting a pension to those persons would be well received by the other classes of society.
Now, I urge the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) as well as the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) and their advisors to consider thoroughly the matter and I hope that we will soon have a legislation reducing the retirement age at 60 and that it will not merely be a promise.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ELIGIBILITY OF PERSONS AGED 60 TO 65 FOR OLD AGE SECURITY PENSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure for me to take part in this debate, in view of the importance of the motion moved by members of the Social Credit. I think that this motion is a great idea as it is very important for the country, and I feel that it concerns the majority of members, if not all.
I have had the pleasure of making some remarks on the necessity of a pension at 60. There were at that time two reasons for such a policy, and I believe that after about one and a half years, I have had the opportunity, four or five times, of advocating the passing of such a measure. In fact, I find today that this idea seems more and more in agreement with the view of several hon. members, and I think that in the present context, such a solution would allow us to improve in no small way the present situation of employment.
I may have to repeat some comments that I have already made in this House. As a matter of fact, there are many reasons why the government should give serious consideration to this policy in the interest of the aged in the whole Canadian economy.
We take the opportunity that this allotted day affords us to make hon. members sensitive to this motion. I also believe that, because of hon. members' participation, the government will be inclined to give more attention to the matter than it has done so far.
Of course, one must admit at the start that there will be a price to pay. I believe that any social measure calls for some sacrifice, but, if they assess the effect of such a measure, most hon. members will not hesitate to vote the required funds, considering the way in which such a measure will help give new stability to the economy of the world in which we are now living.
We can link it of course, with the current social climate, but I think the measure cannot be more justified and the figures I could quote were already given in this House. One thing is sure, however; through such a measure we could reduce the unemployment rate by about 60 or 70 per

October 21, 1971
Old Age Security Pensions
cent. And if we calculate the costs to the state of maintaining 600,000 or 700,000 unemployed, we should all the more reconsider this possibility and I can well imagine that a drop of 50 p. cent in the number of unemployed would enable the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) to sleep soundly. It would equally enable the hon. Minister of National Healh and Welfare (Mr. Munro) to be happier. We should appreciate their efforts to improve the present situation, but, being realistic, we should at the same time recognize that their achievements have not met our expectations and due to the unavailability of the cure-all which we are always seeking, I think that the policy of providing old age security pensions at the age of 60 would offer a far easier solution than we have been hitherto contemplating.
I think that we have neglected to seriously consider this policy which appears too simple at first glance, but in the end, it would contribute to the greater happiness of a specific category of citizens as it would rekindle hope in the younger generation now awaiting the openings that the government has been unable to provide. Should we blame only the government? I do not think so because the situation is difficult everywhere.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that if they undertook a little investigation in various regions, all hon. members would realize that those who are pushing "60" or who are already in their 60's, would be most favourable to such pensions, considering the difficulties encountered by workers. Machines are constantly encroaching on the activities of man who normally, at that age, wishes to be provided with an adequate pension.
I believe it would be most convenient to consider the passing of a bill which would bring about that old age security. It might be better perhaps to introduce such a measure on a voluntary basis for the first six months, so as to enable people with a sufficient income-I mean by that, an amount of $150 as suggested by an hon. member of the NDP, amount which would surely not be too much, considering the fact that a pensioned couple would receive $300 per month, and that unemployed people receive more than $300 per month-to make a decision.
I believe we should consider that seriously so as to enable those older people to remain an asset in our society, to live a happier life under the present circumstances, recognizing at the same time all the benefits such a measure would provide, thus creating a much more valid social context than the one we know at the present time.
I shall limit myself to those few comments as I have been aware for a long time of the benefit of such measure and I hope the hon. members here will make an enquiry in their constituency and will all unhesitatingly claim from the people responsible in the department concerned, from the cabinet and from Parliament, the establishment of such a measure, to put the world back on its feet, by giving holidays to people who deserve them, creating employment for young people who have been longing for it for such a long time, which would make them much more optimistic as to the future, considering the comparisons we could make and the present difficulties they must face.
I will limit myself to those few remarks, but I cannot help denying the comments made a while ago to the effect that such a policy could be established over a five-year period.
I believe the present economic difficulties are much more urgent than the introduction of a legislation to cover the people who would be 60 years of age only in five years from now.
I think we will have to move at a faster pace than we did when we lowered the pensionable age from 70 to 65 years of age, and keeping in mind once again the present economic difficulties, I think the 12-month or perhaps six-month period could be left to the discretion of any worker wanting to take advantage of an adequate pension and quit working. He would still have a six-month period to make room for younger people who are costing the government plenty and at the same time, it would allow those who deserve holidays after working for 25, 30 or 40 years to be assured of a security the younger generation is already thinking about. I think that those who are now nearing the sixty mark have well deserved this treatment which would be the most human one the government would have ever given.
Together with the other hon. members of this House, I suggest that the government seriously consider implementing this policy as soon as possible in the best interests of all those who deserve it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ELIGIBILITY OF PERSONS AGED 60 TO 65 FOR OLD AGE SECURITY PENSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the subject matter of the motion moved by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) is of great concern to all of us, as it is to me.
The subject matter of that motion, old age security pensions, is undoubtedly a very important issue respecting which we all feel highly concerned. So I am very pleased to have this opportunity to make my views known in the House this afternoon and to express my opinion on that motion, to say what I think of it, and how we should deal with this problem.
The proposed motion consists of two parts. What strikes me in the first one is that it sets out to blame the government. As a matter of fact, it reads:
-that the government has not deemed advisable to provide old age security pensions to persons between the ages of 60 and 65,-
As it was pointed out to us a moment ago by the hon.. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), we are going to be told that so much has been done in the past, and I do agree with that.
I feel I can assert that those governments which extended social security to cover not just older people but also the weak, the sick, the widowed, in short, all the underprivileged, have always been Liberal governments.
I extend my congratulations to the hon. member for Roberval for having introduced this motion, for we cannot but support any suggestion aimed at improving our pension system for older people.
However, there is one aspect of this I should like to emphasize and which I find quite sensible, and that is the way we should provide for the wife of a pensioned older citizen. We all have in our respective constituencies-at least I have met many in mine-older couples who have

October 21, 1971

always done their utmost to earn a living, who have lived with pride and dignity. Two or three weeks ago, I had such a couple in my office on a visit: the husband, 65 years old, is a pensionner. Although he would like to keep on working just like before, he is no longer able to do so because of a recent illness. Therefore, his only income is his pension.
His wife who is 59 has always lived on her husband's income, looking after the household and her family. Because of her age, she can expect very little assistance from her provincial Department of Health, Family and Social welfare. This couple have barely enough to live on and both of them are disheartened and saddened by what is happening to them. And in spite of all their efforts and all the requests they make to improve their lot, because of the existing laws and regulations, they get nowhere.
This is why we should urge the government that this specific point of the motion be given our consideration or be efficiently studied by the department involved and the officials who usually take care of such requests.
As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said, this system should obviously be regulated. An older man may have a much younger wife. I know this is unusual. Sometimes, this woman works to make a living and some unbalance would result if this comparatively young working woman received the old age security pension. The same reasoning applies to opposite situations.
As regards pension eligibility at 60, which would enable older people to lead a more human life in security, with the same living standards as the others, we all agree that we should keep on doing something in that direction.
Besides, our democratic institutions remind us of those principles in the Bill of Rights. May I read section 25 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights of 1948, and I quote:
Everyone has the right to a standard of living adequate for the health and well-being of himself and of his family, including food, clothing, housing and medical care and necessary social services, and the right to security in the event of unemployment, sickness, disability, widowhood, old age or other lack of livelihood in circumstances beyond his control.
All those philosophical principles concerning social security, guaranteed income, assistance to the sick, are shared by everyone. However, opinions are divided, even among the people, at least in my region. I have met people who criticize-and sometimes rightly-certain social security measures, saying that in certain cases they might encourage some of the welfare recipients to commit a capital sin which I will not mention, since everybody here knows about it.
However, others who are really in need, who would really want to live in dignity as proud citizens, cannot get enough.	[DOT]
In any event, it would be desirable, as other members have said, to give immediately a very large amount, either $150 a month or more, to older people. But I think that all responsible citizens, even the older ones who want these amounts to better their lot, realize that a government cannot pay out so much money overnight, because it would throw our economy out of balance.
Old Age Security Pensions
Those projects that we all consider with much eagerness and sincerity can nevertheless be developed within a certain period. At the present time, people say that even if the government has not been able to give the aged everything some require, it has found money to encourage, in other fields, other active and productive citizens. Of course, it had to be done. I have in mind the unemployed who are able to work and who are looking for a job.
In conclusion, I would like to stress the following point: Whatever may be said, it is always easier to find solutions which are sometimes over-simple to problems that are rather complicated, as everybody admits. If it were that easy, the problem of the old age security pension would have been solved like all the other increasingly complicated problems which exist in our technical and modern society.
Thus, in spite of our sincerity and emotion about this, because we all have older people in our families, we can nevertheless ask the government to give special attention to this motion, although we know that the only way we can find practical answers in as short a time as possible is by putting this problem in the hands of scientists and technicians, so that it may be solved by experts with modern, scientific methods. Thus, if we forget about demagogy, if we stop thinking only of elections and start giving some thought to the aged, we will certainly be able to solve this problem.
We are sure, given this government's sincerity and competence, that the problem is going to be solved-as it already is to a great extent.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to say a few words on the motion before us. This is a motion accepted by all hon. members and to which there was almost no opposition. In view of the fact that, generally all members are in favour of this motion, I would now like to suggest new ways and means of implementing its proposals. It is well and fine to talk about them but problems must be solved and funds must be found. In our present system, one must know where to find the necessary funds and how much the financing of such a project may cost.
We already know, Mr. Speaker, that our country can afford to pay to our older people as soon as they reach 60, a reasonable pension to allow them to retire from the work force in order to give others an opportunity to work and, after that, to live as men must live in a wealthy country.
Economic growth must be an economic right which is, first of all, to meet the needs of each Canadian citizen. By his labour and his genius, man has always tried to give a

October 21, 1971
Old Age Security Pensions
larger development to his life. But today, thanks to science and technology, he has become master of practically all nature and is extending his domination increasingly.
Thanks to the proliferation of communication between nations, the human family has become aware of itself as a unique community in the midst of the universe and is gradually so organising itself. As a result, Mr. Speaker, man now owes to his own industry many goods which he formerly awaited from superior forces.
Facing these alternatives and the huge enterprise extending to the whole Mankind, many questions have arisen among men as to the meaning and the value of this diligent activity, what use is to be made of all these new resources, what is the purpose of individual and collective effort, the intensification and the awareness of the needs for development and the personal renascence of a generation liberated by science, Progress and unprecedented wealth, and exceptional national economic growth in
One must admit that manpower needs are dwindling all the time, people being more and more replaced by the machine. Having to face this dilemma, young people remain without employment and older people are forced to cling to their jobs because they have no other source of income.
Another motion is officially put to the House asking that the old age security pension be granted to our citizens when they reach 60 years of age and that it be high enough to enable all citizens over 60, as well as their wives, to lead a decent life in line with their needs and the national production.
We are therefore requesting an increase in the basic pensions, that is more than $80 a month, and a lowering of the age of eligibility from 65 to 60. We also feel indirectly entitled to indicate to the government the means to provide the amounts required for the monthly payment of these pensions.
Within the frame of our economic system and of the present policy, we know that we of the Social Credit will not have our demands met because we are promoting a specific financing technique. Since we do not have the financing power, we are compelled to comply and to suggest means of payment consistent with the present system.
Although we are on the opposition side, although we are a party, that does not prevent us from thinking, from paying taxes, from living and from advising the government according to the custom of the capitalistic system.
We are perfectly aware that we live in Canada in 1971 within the capitalistic system which was generated and has evolved for 100 years under the guidance of the main political parties, the liberal and the progressive conservative parties. We are perfectly aware that we cannot administer nor can we advise the Canadian government as if it were already thinking in terms of social credit. Nevertheless, even under our present system, it is possible to provide better care for human beings, for the citizen, from his birth to his death, from the cradle to the grave, from his first breath to his last.

That is, Mr. Speaker, what must be brought home in Parliament to the 30 ministers and all the elected representatives of the people, in order to provide a fair and efficient administration to 22 million Canadians.
Let us rejoice that our potential production is worth several billion dollars more each year. However, it pains us all to see our best citizens deprived of their fair share of this wonderful production and this, because of our unconcern, our carelessness, our improvidence or incompetence.
Under our present system, we have been able to produce goods worth $90 billion up to 1971. I say $90 billion, but I think that the amount will exceed $92 billion, that is more than $4,200 per capita or $21,000 per household of five.
It is also under our present system that we must be able to organize the distribution, the consumption and the purchasing power of all our citizens, that all might have a fair share of the tremendous national production to which they are entitled.
Let us remember the years 1930-39, the years of the depression. Can we remember the war years, from 1939 to 1945? Can we recall the splendid period of the after-war, when money was plentiful until 1958, when the people started to speak of inflation, of unemployment and poverty, and this, in times of peace and overproduction?
We see clearly that the problems of unemployment, poverty and inflation are not a mere problem of production, but one of distribution. We produce more and more, and consume less and less. This is what is paradoxical about the management of Canada in 1971. We produce a lot, we capitalize too much, and we do not consume enough. There is a nationwide economic imbalance between production, consumption and capitalization. So, we must restore some balance in all this, within the framework of our monetary, economic and political, Canadian and capitalist system of free enterprise.
Here is a very simple table which will make us clearly understand how our national economy is planned by all the leaders, known or unknown, who control our economy. In 1945, 90 per cent of a $12 billion production was consumed and 10 per cent was capitalized. Everybody was happy. In 1958, that is 13 years later, $32 billion were produced, 75 per cent consumed and 25 per cent capitalized. People were still rather satisfied. Today, 13 years later, after the war, $90 billion are produced, but only 60 per cent are consumed and 40 per cent capitalized, mainly in the large companies, private or public institutions and corporations. By keeping the same pace in 1975, we will produce over $140 billion, but we will consume less than 50 per cent and capitalize over 50 per cent. Such a situation is ridiculous.
Still a little later, we will produce $200 billion but the companies will keep 90 per cent of the capitalization and leave only 10 per cent for consumption.
That is where we should intervene, Mr. Speaker. So, in 1971, we face a very well known and definite situation in which the great wealth of Canada and its main banking,

October 21, 1971

business, financial, and industrial institutions is obvious. Apart from those encouraging facts, we notice many deficits in the budgets of several governments, many companies and numerous families which get more and more into debt each year although they still are short of the things necessary to lead a normal life in a country as prosperous as Canada.
These are not joking matters. We are at a loss to understand anything. The entire Canadian population is only able to consume $54 billion of a national product valued at $90 billion, whilst a few corporations and individuals accumulate capital to the tune of more than $36 billion for the years to come, as reserves to guard against risks and guarantee their business security.
Before allowing our firms to set aside surpluses of $36 billion, could we not earmark $12 billion to increase the purchasing power or to guarantee a minimum income to citizens who are deprived of the bare necessities of life as are our 60-year-old senior citizens and others and when such a marvelous national product exists side by side with a highly ambitious capitalization on the part of large corporations.
I am neither against profits and surpluses nor against necessary reserves aimed at guaranteeing business security. I know that this is good. But the evil lies in the abnormal increase in these famous reserves, year after year, on a scale authorized by the ministers and hon. members who have been elected by the people to administer justice and equity for the benefit of consumers who are all entitled to live in Canada, in 1971, in accordance with the national product and before exorbitant reserves have been accumulated for the years to come.
Even when the Bank of Canada was established in 1934, and oftentimes since then, the government has been requested to scrutinize those famous reserves accumulated by banks and corporations and to restrict them or bring them down to a level more in line with reality.
It should be realized that these enormous reserves derive from exaggerated profits obtained through high prices paid by the people. They even constitute the main source of inflation. The statistics published these last years on the secret, discreet and concrete reserves of large companies show that the price increases equal the increased reserves of those companies.
It would take too long to prove this here but the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) is aware of it and so are the accountants, economists and directors of major institutions. All the price increases the population had to put up with from 1960 to 1970 are equal to the accumulation of exorbitant reserves as shown in the report of private and public companies, banks and major institutions.
For the time being and for the purposes of the motion moved today, since better pensions must be paid to those older people of 60 and over, let us not try to determine where the money will be coming from. Money we have plenty. Production is there but it is the purchasing power that is inadequate. The money that is lacking is precisely the money that is needlessly accumulated in the large hidden reserves of major private and public institutions, with the permission or connivance of our government,
Old Age Security Pensions
which is not dishonest, but too unconsciously devoted to old administrative methods of protection, capital or productivity promotion.
Why produce 10 times more if the population does not have more money to buy that increased production? Can anybody answer me? If we produce $90 billion in 1971, we can only consume $54 billion, and other individuals and companies can capitalize $36 billion. If we were to produce $10 billion more, the citizens without purchasing power could not buy this additional production. The trouble is not lack of production but lack of purchasing power to meet the needs of the citizens of all levels and ages, including the children, the students, the unemployed, the crippled, the sick, the mothers with a family, the old, the citizens 60 years old or over who cannot find work and must live in 1971.
As can be seen, the entire economy of this country is off balance: some lack the essentials of life while others enjoy exorbitant surpluses, personally or through their millionaire companies.
People comment on inflation, unemployment, poverty, boosted taxes and prices. Nobody is satisfied. Nonetheless, Canada not enjoys prosperity but ranks among the wealthiest countries in the world. Only an over-all revision is required to restore the economic balance between the various sectors of our population, but we balk at the necessary decision.
The United States again will take the lead. They are now taking steps so that conflicts between employers and employees will be settled before the consumers, who at last will have their say and an opportunity to take exception to the price increases due to the increases in wages and interests rates.
Production is intended for consumption. Without consumers, there would be no need for production. But if consumers have no purchasing power, no money to buy production, it is not much better. Our lopsided system is not comfortable with those dependent consumers requesting pension, allowances or grants that they manage to have productive citizens pay through their income derived from wages or interests.
The solution would simply be to have the huge reserves capitalized yearly by big companies converted into purchasing power for dependent citizens. There would be no need then to increase personal income taxes, the cost of living, the price of products or services. This will have to be done sooner or later. It is not a matter of overtaxing corporations but of taxing their tremendous reserves and their reported profits. That is the important thing.
Today when individuals pay $5 in taxes, corporations pay only $1. We shall have to set this straight some day if we want a fair tax system. After ten years of studies and a royal commission on taxation, this point perhaps the only important one, was overlooked.
On page 113 of the bulky report of the Carter Commission on taxation, Mr. Carter took exception to the "practices" used in computing the depreciation reserves of the corporations, but no one wants to mention this dissenting opinion of the chief commissioner himself-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree that there should be improvements in the old age pension program, but I do not agree with this motion. The motion suggests, among other things, that the basic pension is the old age security pension. This is not true. At the present time the foundation, the core of our old age pension program is the Canada Pension Plan plus the old age security pension.
The motion also suggests an extension of the flat rate, universal old age security payment, in other words an extension of the basic $80 a month which is not related to other income and is not related to contributions. I totally reject a flat increase in the universal old age security of $80 a month. I think there is no justification for paying government pensions to all individuals without consideration of their other income, their other pensions, their rents, their dividends, their profits, and so on.
During the debate today the hon. member for Vancouv-er-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) stated that if we increased the old age security pension for everyone we could get back all this money from the rich through income taxes. As a matter of fact, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway asked why the government cannot get it all back from recipients who are wealthy, through the income tax system. A few years ago when we introduced the guaranteed income supplement the minister produced statistics to show that you do not get it all back through the income tax system.
I cannot agree to the payment of a flat rate to everyone, hoping to get it back in some cases through the income tax system when through the very simple procedure of the guaranteed income supplement we can pay out money to the people who need it most. I think we should take the money that is available and divide it among those who have none or very little private income so that they can have a decent pension.
This year we are spending $2.2 billion on old age security and guaranteed income supplements. If we divided this among all our pensioners, rich and poor, the guaranteed minimum of $135 a month would not be available. In other words, if we divided that $2.2 billion among all the pensioners, the average pension would be below $135. We can only pay the $135 minimum because we are being selective.
I said that the Canada Pension Plan is the core of our old age pension program. When it comes fully into effect in 1976 under the present legislation we will be paying $121 per month to persons who have annual earnings of $5,200 a year. That $121 a month, plus the basic old age security of $80, would provide a pension of $201 a month. I said that this would be the case under the present legislation, Mr. Speaker, because in its white paper the government proposes changes in the Canada Pension Plan. For example, it proposes that by 1976 we would have a pension of $162 per month for those with average annual
[Mr. Latulippe.J
earnings of approximately $7,000, and if we add the basic $80 old age security pension to that it will give a pension of $242 a month.
When he introduced the white paper the minister said the changes proposed to the Canada Pension Plan were subject to negotiation with the provinces, especially with the province of Quebec because the Quebec Pension Plan is very closely tied in with the Canada Pension Plan. I hope the minister will proceed quickly with these negotiations and that very soon he will get acceptance for his proposals.
These figures I have given are for the Canada Pension Plan when it comes fully into effect in 1976. In this coming year, however, 1972, a person whose average annual earnings are $5,200, which is the maximum, will receive $65 a month from the Canada Pension Plan, plus $80 a month from old age security and $22.50 from the guaranteed income supplement. He will receive part of the income supplement because his income other than the old age pension will be less than $110 a month, so that the total he will receive in 1972 will be $171.50 a month, which is more than the $150 suggested by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre on a flat, universal basis.
I also wish to point out that the estimate with respect to the Canada Pension Plan is that it will cover 92 per cent of all employees and self-employed persons. The Canada Pension Plan also has a 2 per cent cost of living escalation clause. As I say, this is the core of our pension program. For those who will not have a sufficient number of working years, or who could not work at all, we have the guaranteed income supplement and the Canada Assistance Plan. The guaranteed income supplement at the present time provides $55 a month for those who have no other income.
The number of persons who are now receiving the guaranteed income supplement will become less as time goes by because more and more people will be covered by the Canada Pension Plan. Then as more people become covered by the Canada Pension Plan they will receive that plus the old age security and they will be getting the type of pension I referred to a few minutes ago which, for the vast majority of Canadians, if the proposals of the minister go through, would be approximately $242 a month in 1976.
The present old age security, guaranteed income supplement and the Canada Pension Plan are payable at age 65. Those who retire before 65 must rely on the Canada Assistance Plan and the programs that are related to it. I would favour reducing the qualifying age for the Canada Pension Plan, but not for the old age security as suggested in this motion. I suggest that one could take advantage of the Canada Pension Plan at age 60 in the same way that persons can now take advantage of it at age 65, that is if they leave the work force and retire. Under the present Canada Pension Plan, between ages 65 and 70 you do not get the pension, or you may get only part of it if you work between those ages, but at age 70 you get it in full whether you work or not. I would make that plan applicable at age 60. But the important difference between my proposal and that in the motion is that I would apply it to the Canada Pension Plan because, as I have said, it is the core of our pension program. It is based on contributions and
October 21, 1971

the benefits are much higher than they are under the flat rate, universal old age security pension.
The motion proposes that wives at any age should receive old age security if their husbands have retired. I cannot accept that proposal. In many cases wives work and earn good incomes. There are cases where the wife wants to work. I can see no reason for paying a pension to a wife who is under 60, say 50 or 45, if she is working, just because her husband is retired. I would suggest, in its place, that she have the right as of age 60 to receive the old age pension if her husband is retired. Of course, if she had worked in her lifetime she would be eligible for the Canada Pension Plan and could receive those benefits at age 60, just as her husband could. If she had not worked at all, the only thing she could rely on would be the old age security pension. I would agree that if she is not working at age 60 she should have the right to the old age security pension.
I want to raise two matters with which I am not satisfied in the present program. One is the 2 per cent cost of living escalation clause. On several occasions in the House I have said that I do not think it is reasonable to limit the cost of living escalation clause to 2 per cent. I believe it should be the same as the percentage increase in the cost of living. The 2 per cent figure was picked when we introduced the Canada Pension Plan. At that time the minister said we would fix it at 2 per cent because in some years the cost of living rose and in others it went down. That might be true if we look at statistics over the last 50 years, but if we look at statistics since the last war I do not think there was any occasion when the cost of living dropped below that of the previous year. So if the 2 per cent was based on the fact that we will have reductions in the cost of living, I think it is unreasonable.
We should be prepared to increase pensions automatically in accordance with the total increase in the cost of living. This would be paid for by the increase in income tax collected due to increased wages. I think we should able to pay for a total increase in the cost of living under the guaranteed income supplement and under the Canada Pension Plan. If we are to do that and we want a reasonable pension for the small group of people not eligible for the Canada Pension Plan, then I think the guaranteed income supplement should also be increased to $70 a month.
That would mean a guaranteed minimum pension of $150 a month instead of $135. It would not be, as suggested by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, the basic, universal old age security which is paid to everyone but, rather, it would be as a result of the guaranteed income supplement. As I said before, this would be a better use of the money available for old age security.
I realize that to have a total increase in the pension fixed to the cost of living, and to increase the supplement to $70 a month would be costly. I also realize that in this fiscal year we are spending $2.2 billion on old age security. That is a lot of money. I understand the difficulty of the government in raising money for programs at this time. However, I put forward these proposals because I
Old Age Security Pensions
think they are goals that we have to achieve and I think they can be achieved if we put our minds to it.
Mr. Speaker, I have referred to the Canada Pension Plan, the old age security and the guaranteed income supplement but I have not mentioned private pensions. In Canada, most companies now have private pension programs and the great majority of them do not have a cost of living escalation clause. Some of them have accepted such clauses. As a matter of fact, this House made a report last year or the year before with respect to the Canadian National Railways and when they revised their pension plan our proposal to include a cost of living escalation clause was accepted. The public service of Canada also has an escalation clause in its pension plan. I think it would help to reduce social tensions and bring about a much happier generation of elderly people if more private companies included a cost of living escalation clause in their pension programs. Several have done it and I see no reason why more should not.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to repeat my points. First, I do not think we should increase the basic universal pension of $80 a month; I think that should remain fixed. Second, I think that the core of our pension program should continue to be the Canada Pension Plan, and I hope the government will get agreement for the changes proposed in its white paper as soon as possible. Third, I suggest that the age of eligibility under the Canada Pension Plan should be 60 years, but only if the person was not working, or in the same manner in which it is now available between the ages of 65 and 70 years.
Fourth, women over 60 years of age should be eligible for the old age security pension if the husband is retired. I do not think they should be eligible for a pension if they are under 60 years of age and working. Fifth, if women are under 60 years of age I think they should be eligible if they are not working and their husband is on the guaranteed income supplement. That would give some reason for paying the pension to a woman under 60 years of age because it would mean that the family income was not high and there could be a situation where the woman could not obtain work.
Six, I think if we want to make the guaranteed income supplement more in tune with today's cost of living, it should be $70 a month. This would mean that the guaranteed minimum pension would be $150 instead of $135. If we had that as well as an escalation clause which would increase with the cost of living, then I think we would have a first-class pension package. By that I mean one basically founded on the Canada Pension Plan and which would provide a guaranteed income supplement for the small percentage of people not eligible for the Canada Pension Plan.

I thank you Mr. Speaker. I did not expect to speak so early, but I am pleased to welcome this opportunity.
I do not very often have the opportunity to speak in the House for the simple reason that the opposition members have so much to say that there is scarcely any time left for the government members. In spite of all that, we are criticized.
I must also add that if certain opposition members feel unable to communicate with the government, they are the only ones to blame. As for me, I have good relationships I should even say fruitful ones and generally satisfactory.
Since the government is also made up of men and therefore can make mistakes at times, sin through omission, accomplish too little or not enough,-depending of course on which side of the House the members are,-it is easy, much too easy, for a member of the opposition to blame the administration, to blame the government for not looking after the older people as it should. Politically speaking, this may seem profitable, but I must confess that I can do without this kind of politicians who quite irresponsibly, make use of the conditions or circumstances of older people in order to get political support. I have not accused anyone, Mr. Speaker. The truth is that there is not a single member in this House who is uninterested in the old people's lot. On the contrary, I am sure we are all endeavouring to find the means to provide our old people with a happy and peaceful retirement.
The hon. members, Mr. Speaker, are not the only ones to tackle this problem. Let us not forget the many agencies, associations and religious orders that were active in this field before governments even thought of acting.
Every one of us has in his family, among his friends and acquaintances some aged persons. We cannot forget even for a moment the needs of those persons. Many of them

were able to provide for themselves during their years of retirement an adequate income from their earnings during their best years of activity. Many live very well, but it goes without saying that there are many in our country who do not have the bare minimum, others who, having saved all through their life, find that, with the cost of living, their savings are not enough. And the saddest thing is to see an older person, an aged couple afflicted by illness.
We must ask ourselves very seriously if our senior citizens, our present pensioners, whoever they are, whatever area of this country that they live in, have all they need to live decently. Being realistic I feel that we could do more for the aged, before thinking of forcing into retirement people who have not reached the required age and who are still productive.
I have often discussed this question with my constituents. Some tell me that the problem of unemployment can be solved by retiring 60 year-old people. I am not aware of all the consequences that such a measure might have on our economy, but I have a distinct feeling that our economy and productivity, and consequently the revenues of governments, would suffer from it. People between 60 and 65 have reached the top of the salary scale. They have quite often acquired an experience difficult to replace, and I fear that it would be disastrous for our economy if these Canadians were to prematurely leave the labour force for an early retirement.
However, I do not reject completely the concept of people being pensioned at 60. In every sector of commercial, industrial, professional and even parliamentary activity-for we have here relatively aged members who should have retired a long time ago, people who often say they are marking time-
