speechtext:
Long before they reach retirement age, some people mark time, that is they keep count of how many years, months, weeks and even days there are before they retire. Consequently, they gradually lose interest in their profession and their work. They become less productive and have a tendency to be more critical of their employers, to get on their colleagues' nerves at work without rhyme or reason, finally to become a nuisance to everybody. They mark time and occupy positions that would be more properly filled by young people entering the labour market. Those people whose only concern is an early retirement could be encouraged. I think that would be profitable to the Canadian economy. However, it should be done gradually and systematically and with great discretion. I would suggest that governments and large corporations first make a limited experiment the results of which should be assessed.
A great number of Canadians are fed up helping those who could work but are too lazy to do so when jobs are available. The payment of welfare allowances to young
October 21, 1971

people able to work is beginning to exasperate the taxpayers. We will soon reach the revolt level, if governments fail to solve this problem. And I do not have that solution, Mr. Speaker. Frankly, I do not believe that the solution proposed today by the Social Credit is entirely acceptable. In any event, not now. It might be practicable in a rich province, like Ontario, but certainly not in New Brunswick where less and less salaried people are called upon to support more welfare recipients.
We are faced with serious problems in the social field. We all recognize it. However, all men of good will, all well intentioned governments must pool their resources to find solutions that will be satisfactory to the majority of Canadian taxpayers. Study groups, committees and white papers must be included in the exercise. But in the final analysis, each government must take realistic decisions. Motions such as the one introduced today are not the solution. I feel that the proposal is too oversimplified and therefore, I cannot support it.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Ouellet) will be closing the debate. I have much confidence in the young member for Papineau and I am eager to hear him. But before resuming my seat, I would ask him to discuss with the minister the possibility of extending the coverage of the old age security system to those individuals who, having not yet reached the conventional age of retirement, have become unable to earn their living, due to illness, disability or any other valid reason. There are plenty of such cases in these days of heart attacks, nervous breakdowns, accidents of all kinds and incurable diseases.
However, I would like to tell the Parliamentary Secretary that in my view it would be premature to set up a universal pension plan at age 60. Let us first of all look after the really old people and then we can think of spending additional sums of money for people 60 or over.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ELIGIBILITY OF PERSONS AGED 60 TO 65 FOR OLD AGE SECURITY PENSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was afraid that after all the speakers to whom you gave the floor I could not get a few words in, at least, on the motion I was pleased to support this afternoon.
The motion is extremely simple and important. It purports to make all those who are 60 or over eligible for the old age security pension.
Mr. Speaker, I should now like to draw a parallel. A few days ago, the Solicitor General (Mr. Goyer) announced his department's policy concerning rehabilitation of inmates. He said here in the House that such rehabilitation was most important. Thus the Solicitor General apparently wanted to make available to inmates the promises of the just society, whereas the majority of our old people in Canada will unfortunately have to wait too long, particularly those in whose behalf we presented this motion today.
If we are going to be so considerate towards prisoners in Canada, it seems to me that we should be even more so towards people 60 years of age or over. It is with this purpose in mind that tonight I gladly second the motion proposed by my colleague, the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier).
Old Age Security Pensions
Mr. Speaker, we in Canada-as everyone knows-live in affluence: we are constantly being told that we have too much wheat, too many dairy products, too many agricultural products, too much fuel, too many textile products, too many building materials, too many slums, too many farmers, too many workmen, too many teachers. On the other hand, we also have 650,000 unemployed too many- including educated ones-too many illiterate people, too many retrained people, too many poor, too many industries which do not run to their full potential, too many empty pockets, too many bankruptcies, too many debts and too many taxes, as well as too many old people who live in poverty.
When a man turns 50, it is true today that he cannot find employment in Canada. Nor does he like to beg the mere pittances of social welfare. He wants to work and not to live off public charity. If our economy cannot give him a job, it seems to me we could pay him a pension at 60, especially when we know that, in most cases, those people brought up seven or eight children.
The government should revise its social policy along those lines. They would thus give opportunities to the young who in turn want to have a family and have the privilege of doing what others had a chance to do before them.
Today, Mr. Speaker, a young person who is unemployed is a candidate for protestation and also, perhaps, unfortunately, a candidate for revolution.
Mr. Speaker, the 60 year old man and woman are cast aside. Thus we take away from them their privilege as respected human beings in our society by imposing upon them a social life pattern where often and unfortunately they are rudely treated. They must suffer the humiliation of being rejected as useless by a selfish and unfair society while, during the electoral campaign in 1968, we had them dream of a just society which is yet to come.
Often, we unfortunately blame the elderly people for their age. If the pension begins at 65, old age begins however at hiring, that is at 40, because at 50 no job is available anywhere. According to reports of the Department of Manpower and Immigration, we must let the young work but, unfortunately, today the place of 40 year old people in our society is often in the welfare office.
Mr. Speaker, that motion proposes that pensions be paid from the age of 60 for many reasons, because after having worked for over 40 years, those same people often feel tired and are no longer able to do their job properly. And others can no longer work due to poor health. They also would like to enjoy some comfort, to live it up, to travel before the end of their lives.
Mr. Speaker, in these days of unemployment, young people should be allowed to replace their elders in the labour force.
If we gave the old age pension to the 60-year olds, we would automatically reduce the number of unemployed who, unfortunately, include too many young people. We would be surprised at the number of young people who would work. It would not cost the government more to give pensions to those citizens 60 years of age.
Moreover, with the implementation of the recommendations contained in the motion, many people would be
8914

October 21, 1971
Old Age Security Pensions
pleased to keep their aged parents with them. According to the stupid social welfare legislation we know, particularly in the province of Quebec, those who would like to keep and maintain their parents would be no longer eligible to any social welfare allowance. If welfare services agree to help them, the amount allowed is reduced to the bare minimum.
If the aged are living with strangers, or alone in a small apartment, welfare services grant them the full pension and pay all drugs and care.
These laws are stupid, they force children to neglect their aged parents. I personally know of married children who are working and living without any luxury, but who would welcome their aged parents in their home. But the fear of drugs and care costs forces them to be prudent and prevents them from keeping their parents under their own roof.
In 1971, Canada could, I think, pay a pension to the 60-year olds and they could end their days in serenity with the members of their own family instead of living in solitude.
Today, in our society, children are unfortunately in the same position as older people. They do not have their place in our so-called modern society. They seem to embarrass everybody, and this scandal should not be tolerated in our country.
I have with me very interesting data on showing the aging pattern of the population.
In 1951, there was 126,000 people aged 65 or more. In 1961, 306,000. In 1971, 411,000. In 1981, they will be 600,000. And the June, 1970, figures show that in Canada, there are close to 750,000 people aged 60 to 65 who now receive no old age pension at 60.
Senior citizens deserve better than having to worry about tomorrow, worries, financial difficulties, moral hardships and insecurity. They deserve better than having to live on others, all the more as at this age illness and worries about their children are often their major concern.
If we are to have a modern society, we should do better for our old people than the so-called primitive tribes which show more concern about their aged people than we do. At present, certain under-developped countries do more for their people aged 60 and even 50 than we do here in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, it is also quite normal for people aged 60, in the last ten years of their life, that they may enjoy recreational activities in this century of leisure, at a time when automation increasingly reduces working hours, when unemployment is affecting thousands of homes; we should be able in our modern society to enable our senior citizens to enjoy recreational activities.
The motion before us is most simple. The government will probably again use the pretext of expenses, while Canadians can certainly provide the aged people with food, accommodation and comfort, in short, anything we can possibly give them.

But there again we are up against backwards, obsolete and archaic financial conditions. Therefore the members of the Ralliement creditiste are right in saying that Canada is bursting with all sort of riches while our citizens between 40 and 60 years of age cannot find jobs nowhere in Canada. It is high time that this government, the self-declared government of the just society, would at least provide our older citizens with an opportunity to live decently.
This is why I urge the government to study the matter earnestly, because the Creditistes are not alone in asking for the pension to be paid at 60 years of age. For several years, various public bodies and organizations have asked for it. We often read in the newspapers open letters with requests for the payment of the pension at 60 years of age.
Prior to the next federal election, we should be able to say to our 60 year-old people that they are not a privileged group and that we recognize what they have done, for we must not forget that if we can enjoy the comforts and the standard of living we now have, if our society has been developed we owe it mainly to our older citizens.
It is on account of such facts and because we can achieve that physically that the government should not stumble against a mere financial difficulty, that it should get off the beaten track so as to put money at the service of production, production at the service of old people in order that our 60 year-old citizens may be regarded as full-fledged citizens in our economy, benefit from this country's great production and enjoy the last years of their life, especially since they have given so much for this country and for their fellow-citizens.

speakeroldname: Mr. Andre Ouellet (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ELIGIBILITY OF PERSONS AGED 60 TO 65 FOR OLD AGE SECURITY PENSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this week the Social Credit party has taken its "money-printing machine" out of mothballs. Last Monday evening, the leader of the Social Credit party, the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) talked about a guaranteed income plan for all Canadians of 18 and over, regardless of whether they were working or not, had money or not, were millionaires or unemployed. That plan would cost roughly $18 billion, four times more than what is now being spent in the field of social security. With that plan, the annual budget expenditures of the federal government would automatically double.
Now, the Social Credit party is putting forward new proposals for older people in Canada. This new formula would cost over $1.1 billion to the public treasury. As you can see, the Creditiste "money-printing machine" is going at full blast this week.
If we were to grant an old age pension of $80 a month to all older people between 60 and 65, it would cost an additional amount of $740 million in 1972, an increase of nearly 45 per cent over present expenditures.
Furthermore, if we were to extend the guaranteed income supplement to that age group, the combined additional cost of guaranteed income and old age pensions would be roughly $850 million, for a total amount of $3.4 billion in 1972, and that would be for all persons of 60 and over.
The present government is undoubtedly concerned with older people. The record of all Liberal governments in the
October 21, 1971

past has more than proved it, and I think it would be useful to recall the part it has played in the old age security pension plan. The first attempt in Canada to make any kind of government provision for older persons was the passage in 1908 of the Canadian Government Annuities Act.
In 1927 the Old Age Pension Act went into effect. This provided financial assistance to persons 70 years of age or over who could meet a means test. This act was administered by the provinces with a federal sharing of the costs of the pension. At first the federal government contribution was 50 per cent but this was later increased to 75 per cent. In the years that followed after 1927, there were a number of amendments to the Old Age Pensions Act liberalizing the amount of the benefit which originally had been $20 a month to $40 a month and there were changes in the means test requirements as well. Nevertheless it became apparent that there was some dissatisfaction with this method of meeting the needs of older people.
In 1950 there was established a joint parliamentary committee of the House of Commons and the Senate. This committee made an exhaustive study of the various pension schemes then in existence throughout the world and they heard briefs from various organizations and individuals to get any opinions possible as to the best course to be followed in Canada. It is interesting now to read the committee reports of that date and to notice that there was some discussion of the introduction of an insurance plan similar to the Old Age and Survivors Insurance of the United States which had gone into effect in the mid-30's. Coming out of this committee were recommendations to the effect that there should be established a system of universal pensions for persons 70 and over coupled with a program to be called Old-Age Assistance paid on a means test basis for persons 65 to 69 years of age. The federal government would administer and pay for the universal pension while the provinces would administer the Old Age Assistance Act-with the federal government paying 50 per cent of the assistance payment.
The government of the day decided to implement the committee recommendations, but before this could be done it was ncessary to obtain a constitutional amendment which would permit the federal government to legislate concurrently with the provincial governments. This was obtained and the Old Age Security Act of 1951 was passed to become effective January 1952.
The amount which was to be paid under the Old Age Security Act when it was first established in January 1952 was $40 a month. This was changed over the years so that, in July 1957, under a Liberal government, the pension became $46 a month, in November 1957 $55 a month, in February 1962 $65 a month and since October 1963 has been at the rate of $75 a month.
The main premise of the old age security scheme is to pay a pension on a universal basis with no means test and with no direct connection with the financing of the plan. The application for pension does not have any question concerning income or resources. In order to qualify for the pension, the individual needs only to establish that he is of the proper age and that he has met certain residence
Old Age Security Pensions
requirements. In other words, any person who meets the age and residence requirements is eligible for the pension and there is no reference to his income or to any contribution he may have made to the Old Age Security fund in the past, present, or future. It is obvious that the principle of the Old Age Security Act follows more closely the schemes in effect in New Zealand and Sweden, rather than the social insurance approach of the United States and Great Britain. It can be noted, besides, that at present the Canada Pension Plan is based on the social insurance principle.
The plan is operated on a pay-as-you-go basis. The Old Age Security fund receives money through a sales tax, a corporation income tax and a personal income tax. Originally, the formula was 2 per cent for each of these items, subject to a limit of $60 a year for the personal income tax contribution. This is the formula 2-2-2, and those who were concerned with the operation of the program could only hope that the coincidence that this formula sounded like a headache tablet would not bear any omen of difficulties ahead. The financing at present is through a 3 per cent sales tax, a 3 per cent corporation tax and a 4 per cent personal income tax, subject to a limit of $120, thus a 3-3-4 formula.
Since the passing of the Old Age Security Act, there have been years where the financial resources obtained through these taxes have turned out to be insufficient to meet the costs of pensions. Where this has happened temporary loans have been advanced to the fund and these loans have, in turn, been paid off through grants from general revenue. The current situation is that the income is greater than the outgo.
As can be seen, the evolution of old age security through the years is tremendous. One may be interested to learn that old age security pensioners received $1,730,000,000 during the fiscal year ended March 31, 1970, out of a national budget of approximately $14,000,000,000. There are now approximately 1,670,000 old age security pensioners in Canada. From these figures, one can appreciate that the decisions which are reached must be equitable not only to recipients of social security benefits but also to the taxpayers who must pay for all services provided by the government. Unless, of course, we use the moneymaking machine of the Creditistes. As a matter of fact, that is why we must tackle the question with the utmost caution even if, spontaneously, the members of all parties would like to do much more for the aged.
I think that it is important to deal more particularly with the new guaranteed income supplement program. I would like to say a word about it.
Five years ago, in December 1966, the guaranteed income supplement program for old age security recipients was approved by the members of this House. In January 1967, people who were 68 or older and who had no other source of income became eligible for a 40 per cent supplement to their old age security pension-that is, an extra $30 a month. In the three succeeding years the amount of this supplement rose slightly as the cost of living rose, and the whole benefit-old age security and guaranteed income supplement combined-became payable earlier. Presently, people who are 65 or older can receive as much as $135, consisting of $80.00 in old age
24372-5}

October 21, 1971
Old Age Security Pensions
security pension and $55.00 in guaranteed income supplement. This guaranteed income supplement program has proven very effective. Almost half all old age security recipients are drawing some supplement. The figure had now reached more than 830,000. These people submit application forms each January stating what their family income has been in the previous calendar year. In this way we can be sure that the benefits are being paid to those who need them most, the aged people who have little or no other source of income. This program cost $263 million in 1969-1970, and during the current fiscal year it is expected to cost nearly $300 million.
There are two major features of this program which have made it so effective. One is the income test I have just mentioned. This is an impersonal test that does not involve any private investigation of one's living habits or spending habits. It is no more degrading than the income test that all taxpayers must undergo when they file their income tax returns.
The second is the built-in incentive feature. The supplement is not cut back by a dollar for every dollar of income a person has from other sources. It is only cut back by $1 a month for each $2 a month one has from other sources. This leaves an incentive for older people who can supplement their pensions by doing some work to do so. It leaves an incentive for younger people contemplating retirement to save toward that day.
There are those who argue that the OAS pension itself should have been increased. To raise it by $10 a month to $90 in 1971 would have cost us an extra $206 million. We considered it a far better use of resources to concentrate this sum on improving the supplement for low-income old age pensioners. We have therefore suggested raising the supplement for single pensioners by $22 and for married couples by $29 a month, at a net cost of $194 million.
By so doing we have been able to ensure that all persons over 65 will have incomes of at least $1,600 if single, or of $3,000 if married pensioners. We estimate that about 970,000 pensioners are drawing the supplement, including about 470,000 who are getting full supplement.
Mr. Speaker, there appears to be a growing interest in matters relating to retirement at ages below the traditional retirement age of 65. It is advisable, we feel, to know what the Canadian experience with early retirement has been and whether or not any trends toward early retirement can be detected. For this reason, various data sources have to be examined.
There is no apparent trend towards decreased participation in the combined labour force for the age group 55-64. In fact, there has been a general increase in participation since 1951 for that age group. In the case of males only, however, for the age group 55-64, participation has dropped fairly regularly since 1951 and each year since 1966. Female labour force participation, on the other hand, has increased substantially every year except in 1953 and 1970.
For Canadians in the age group 65 to 69, there is a definite trend towards lesser participation in employment. The participation rate for males, in particular, has declined rapidly in the period 1966 to 1970. This likely is a

reflection of the increasing availability of pension income through OAS and CPP for that age group. The Economics and Research Branch of the federal Department of Labour routinely undertakes a number of studies of developments within the field of collective agreements. In the course of this work some attention is given to the provisions relating to pension plans, which, unfortunately could be given only cursory examination. A detailed study in this area is scheduled for the fall of 1972.
The Department of Labour reports that they have recently conducted an examination of 341 collective agreements negotiated during the period July 1st, 1970, to June 30, 1971. Examination of these collective agreements indicates that 70 contracts had negotiated new provisions with respect to pensions and 26 of these contained clauses for early retirement.
The Department of Labour cannot provide information on the nature of the clauses relating to early retirement nor their effect on retirement age experience. Nevertheless, it seems clear that the private pension field is more and more turning its attention to changes which would allow retirement at ages prior to normal retirement ages.
Many Canadian pension plans permit members to retire early provided certain conditions, based on age or service or a combination of both, are met. The most recent survey of pension plans available for public scrutiny was conducted by The National Trust Company in 1969.
The National Trust survey involved 113 employers which had 136 different pension plans in operation covering more than 1 million employees. There were 24 plans (18 per cent of plans surveyed) which permitted an employee to take his pension prior to normal retirement age without the consent or approval of the employer.
It may be, Mr. Speaker, that a trend will become clear in the next few years.
However, I would like to say in closing that if the Canadian government considers it advisable to look after the aged in order to provide them with decent living conditions, it absolutely does not feel, like the Social Credit, that it is timely to retire persons between 60 and 65 years who can still be very useful in the labour force.

speechtext:
The hon. member is perfectly right in saying that we must give more consideration to the elderly people in Canada. The motion now before us asks that pensions be paid to both husband and wife, provided that one of them has reached the age of 60.
A while ago the hon. member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) was accusing the Creditistes of wanting to play around with the money press. I will remind him that in 1962 when I publicly asked for a pension of $100 a month for the elderly, it was then only $55 a month. The hon. member should get that into his head. But I was then called a fool because I asked for $100. Today this Liberal government is boasting that it pays $135 a month. This means that the Liberals have become "$80 a month more foolish" than I was in 1962.
Mr. Ouellet What was the cost of living at that time?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some mention the cost of living at that time. The hon. member for Papineau was saying: "The Creditistes will start operating their moneymaking machine because the cost would be four times as high with their social security program."
The hon. member who travels throughout the province of Quebec, said in Sherbrooke: "The Creditistes are opposed to our helping the underdeveloped countries." The hon. member knows very well that he is lying through his teeth, because we say that we should help underdeveloped countries, but that there is no reason in the world for not helping our provinces, our municipalities, our school boards in the same way, without depriving anyone of anything.
When the hon. member said a few moments ago that it costs $4 billion for social welfare, social security, unemployment insurance, etc., if he wants to take notes, I shall give him statistics. At the present time, $8,735,400,000 are being paid in social assistance, social welfare. The administrative costs are not included in this amount. I am referring to the Ramsay Committee report on social welfare, dated December 22, 1969. These are the most recent figures. This is a submission from the Canadian Association of Tax Studies.
As regards provincial authorities which make a contribution, the figures for 1969 are reported in the DBS Bulletin 68-205 under Provincial Government Finance.
As for the municipalities, their latest contributions date from 1967.
But, from 1967 to 1971, they have increased, and if we add to $8,735,000,000 the administrative costs of all welfare and unemployment insurance offices, the hon. member will realize that we are now getting close to 12 billion dollars!
The plan which I suggested the other day, under which all others would be abolished, would include pensions, unemployment insurance, social welfare which at the present time create countless abuses. For a population of 21,337,000 inhabitants, this program would cost $19,580,945,000. It is therefore not four times more. If the hon.

That program would cost $19 billion and not $18 billion. This is neither four times as much as what it costs now, nor even twice as much. Taking for granted the fact that the provinces and municipalities contribute to the present overall social welfare program, in all honesty, outside of political considerations, on what do we base ourselves?
We know-and the hon. member is aware of it-that we are producing this year $90 billion worth of consumer goods and services. That is the total production and the total national revenue, including the parliamentary secretary's increase, comes to $65 billion. The figures are not mine but those of government statisticians. Therefore there is a $25 billion gap between our production and our revenue. That production exists but we cannot have it because there are no corresponding credits.
When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) announced a credit of $1,070 billion to provide employment, he did not tell us where it would come from. Did he use a money press? No. He merely said: We are going to have $1,070 billion of new credit. Prior to the last war, our national debt was $3 billion; after the war, it was $17 billion. The $14 billion did not come out in thin air. It did not come out of our pockets because we did not have any money. The government came up with sums of money, appropriations. We made war.
We are presently in conflict with the younger generation and we are wondering what to do about it. And the hon. member knows it because when he went to Sherbrooke he could easily see that it was so. The younger generation nowadays is boiling. They have a grudge against us. They

have a grudge against the establishment. Why? Because last summer, 900,000 of them could not find a summer job. The hon. member also knows that if a war was to break out tomorrow we would have a job for each and everyone of them. They are the ones who do not accept the government's position.
Mr. Speaker, it is not by talking the way the hon. member for Papineau was a while ago that we are going to solve our problems. Mr. Speaker, the "money-printing machine" is becoming outmoded. To the extent that the Canadian people produce goods and services-to that same extent, no more but no less-we suggest that the Department of Finance should use the Bank of Canada to obtain equivalent funds and create new sources of credit.
I have been hearing those people speak of a "moneyprinting machine" for the last 32 years. I can hear them bawling. A lot of bawlers! They understand nothing and yet they denounce everything without any reason. What the hon. member said a few moments ago did not prove anything. He got even mixed up in his statistics. He said: "Four times more". My proposal would promote the sale of Canadian goods. We would not less dependent on the United States with regard to exports and the 10 per cent surtax, because our major market, the domestic market, could still be supplied with goods. Industries would then operate normally and new jobs would be created. That would be a solution to unemployment.
We would no longer see abuses like those now rampant throughout Canada: in Quebec, in Ontario and in all the other provinces. And with the new programs which will be implemented, we will be confronted this coming winter with an unbearable economic situation. So let us have solutions. On our part, we are prepared to support logical solutions. I do not have the time this evening to give further details on the cost of a social security plan, but I have the figures. If any hon. member wants a copy of them, I can send him one. They are true figures. If the hon. member for Bonaventure-iles de la Madeleine wants figures, I will give them when I am in his constituency early in November to make sure that the hon. member knows that his constituents are more interested and more informed than he himself has kept them informed since he has been here.
Mr. Speaker, I call it 10 o'clock. So I will close my remarks, and I will come back to them at the next opportunity.

subsubtopic: NATIONAL PARKS-KLUANE GAME SANCTUARY-POSSIBLE SITE OF NEW PARK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 15, I directed the following question to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien):
Can the minister inform the House if the entire Kluane game sanctuary in the Yukon is actively being considered as a site for a national park?
My supplementary question was:
When may we expect a decision from the minister on the setting aside of this outstanding area for national park purposes?
Mr. Speaker suggested that these questions be placed on the order paper, but I felt that in view of their national importance and the need for an early decision to be made I should raise the issue on our so-called ten o'clock show. May I first point out that there is some urgency in the need for establishing additional national parks throughout Canada. An increasing number of Canadians and interested organizations are actively pressing the government for action on the establishing of more national parks. I will not detail the immense value which accrues to Canadians through the establishment of parks but perhaps I should mention the basic purposes of Canada's national parks as defined in the government's 1964 parks policy statement. It is:
To preserve for all time areas which contain significant geographical, geological, biological or historic features as a national heritage for the benefit, education and enjoyment of the people of Canada.
Canada's national parks system began with the establishment of Banff national park in 1885. Since that time we have added 27 national parks to our parks system. There is urgent need for other areas to be set aside as national parks in an effort to round out the system so that it truly represents all the major regions of our country and includes major geographical and ecological features of national significance. There is increasing urgency for the need to complete our parks system while there is still time. The minister several years ago at a conference in Calgary made the following statement:
The national park system in Canada originated here in the west but it has taken too long to extend the system to other parts of Canada, where there is just as great a need and just as exciting opportunities to establish such parks so that all parts of Canada can share in the benefits of what must become a truly national policy. I would like to impress upon you my sense of urgency on
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Boulanger).]
this question of establishing additional national parks. It is estimated that to achieve adequate representation of Canada's heritage at a suitable scale we shall require 40 to 60 new national parks by 1985.
Wheat creates this sense of urgency are two factors. First, the increased cost of acquiring land for park use is reaching prohibitive levels. Second, past experience has shown that areas of natural beauty can quickly be spoiled for potential park use by different problems of economic and social development. Failure to recognize the urgent need for additional parks will mean that one day we will risk reaching the point of no return.
The very principle of conservation demands that we have the foresight and determination to take action needed today so that tomorrow will not be a time for regretting lost opportunities.
I fully endorse this statement made by the minister, but it is becoming obvious that he is ducking the parks issue as it affects several areas of Canada. One of the most important is the need for a national park in the Yukon which will set aside for all time the Kluane game sanctuary. I point out there are national parks in every province of Canada but none in either the Yukon or the Northwest Territories.
I understand that 28 years ago almost all of the newly created 10,000 square mile Kluane game sanctuary in the Yukon was reserved for national park purposes. I ask the minister why there has been such a lengthy delay in establishing this area as a national park. Are the lobbies of the powerful mining industry to take precedence over what could and should be a national reserve for all time? I point out that mineral resources are non-renewable but the resources of an area preserved in a national park are there for all time and will provide a far more stable economic base over the long-run.
The Kluane game sanctuary is one of the unique areas in Canada. It has terrific potential as a national park. It is located in the extreme southwestern tip of the Yukon and on its eastern boundary is parallelled by the Alaska highway for 200 miles. It is one of the most beautiful areas in the north and contains the Saint Elias mountains which are the highest in Canada. Here we find Mount Logan, our highest peak which towers 19,850 feet.
The game sanctuary contains an outstanding number of wild animals and bird species. It contains a vast ice field, the largest in the world outside of the polar regions. This area is easily accessible and can be reached by automobile from Edmonton and by the Alaska ferry system and car from Vancouver and Prince Rupert. A daily jet service to Whitehorse brings this area only a few hours flying time away from the most populated areas of North America.
The Kluane game sanctuary was reserved 28 years ago for national park purpose. To date no action has been taken by this government or past governments in having it set aside as a national park. At the present time the mining industry has been free to operate in sanctuary virtually without restraint. This is in direct violation of national parks principles and objectives. There is no doubt that the mining industry is extremely important in Canada's economy, but I again refer the minister to the statement which he made at the Calgary conference several years ago:
We must have the foresight and determination to take action needed today so that tomorrow will not be a time for regretting lost opportunities.
October 21, 1971

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: NATIONAL PARKS-KLUANE GAME SANCTUARY-POSSIBLE SITE OF NEW PARK
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: NATIONAL PARKS-KLUANE GAME SANCTUARY-POSSIBLE SITE OF NEW PARK
speechtext:
I suggest to the minister that the time to set the Kluane game sanctuary aside for a national park is now. We cannot afford to lose any more of these choice areas through economic exploiters. Already procrastination on the part of this government and other governments has seen some of the most outstanding park areas in Canada lost for all time to future generations. I point out to the minister that we must look to the future and legislate for the future in the wise disposition of our natural resources.
Our national parks system must be extended to the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. The Kluane game sanctuary should be the first step in our national parks program for the north. This park could become one of the major economic assets of the north and, unlike nonrenewable resources such as minerals, we can expect its value and economic return to sharply increase as time goes on. Here, too, we have an asset which can provide employment for a large number of native people who call northern Canada their home. Their natural talents and skills can be utilized in such projects to a far greater degree than in industrial and economic activities which are for the most part foreign to their way of life.
I urge the minister and the government to move without delay on this very important matter. I trust we shall soon see the entire Kluane game sanctuary set aside as another national park to serve the interests of all Canadians both at the present and in the future.

subsubtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-CANADIAN PENSION COMMISSION-POSSIBLE APPOINTMENT OF EXTRA BODIES TO CLEAR BACKLOG OF CASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should point out to hon. members, and especially to our distinguished clutch of visitors in the galleries, that a great show is taking place outside. It has undoubtedly cut down on our attendance. No doubt the attendance is completely to the satisfaction of the party that I represent. I will now move to non-partisan matters.
I bow to nobody as a parliamentarian in paying respect to those of this Parliament who have concerned themselves with veterans affairs and with the treatment of those who did so much for Canada. It is on their behalf, that is to say on behalf of the veterans of Canada, that I make this pitch tonight. I hope nobody will misconstrue it in any way as being sour or partisan or bitter.
I wish to try to do something about what I believe to be an injustice to Canadian veterans, believing that while good legislation has been passed by all parties in this House there are simply not enough people to carry it out and see that those who are entitled to benefits will receive them quickly. I think that if you have to stand in a queue one mile long and shuffle forward awaiting your turn, even if you will receive justice at the head of the queue, justice delayed is justice denied.
The chairman of the Canadian Pension Commission, Mr. Allan O'Solomon, according to a report in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of Wednesday points out that applications under the new act are coming in at the rate of 1,000 a month. In other words, some 7,000 cases have been piled on the doorstep of the Commission since the new legislation came into effect. There are many reasons for this situation. First, any claim which has been denied in the past can be reopened because of the provision made for a shift in the balance of the preponderance of evidence rules which guided the commission in the past. We all fought for that. We are glad to see it in effect, but it means that many claims are being put forward which are unlikely to be dealt with expeditiously in the present circumstances.
Other factors can now be taken into consideration, too. There is the effect of a war disability upon a second disability incurred since war service; there is the special position of those who were prisoners of the Japanese; there is the effect of the new clauses dealing with disability claims and widows claims. So in effect we are dealing with a wholly new situation when it comes to claims which can be presented to the commission, thanks to the generous action of this House. I do not make any claim

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion that I had anything to do with that. Perhaps I did with regard to the evidentiary balance, but otherwise no.
I can see around me hon. members who were engaged in this work and I am proud of the decisions they reached. But if a man is at the back of a queue of 7,000 people he is at the back of a queue which is very long indeed. I therefore make two suggestions for speeding up this whole process so that those affected can obtain their rights. First, there should be consultation between the Department of Veterans Affairs and Bar Associations in various parts of Canada, particularly in areas where large numbers of claims have been filed in order that lawyers may be retained even on a temporary basis to provide what is in effect a free legal counsel which is available to everyone who uses the veterans bureau to present claims.
The other suggestion is this. There must be a method of apppointing special panels even on a temporary basis until we can clear up this overwhelming backlog of cases. This need not be done in all areas; it can be done where the need is most pressing. In some provinces sufficient resources are already available, but if we take a sensible attitude even the 7,000 cases which have arisen since the new legislation became effective could be processed with some kind of expedition. People would not then feel that they were caught forever in the back end of an alley and could not see their way to the front. I make that suggestion to the government and I hope it will be considered.

subsubtopic: MANPOWER-AVAILABILITY OF JOB VACANCY SURVEY DATA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I asked the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Lang) for an explanation of some of the many inefficiencies in his department. Specifically, I asked him why it has taken four years, the employment of 106 bureaucrats and the spending of more than $3 million to produce a report about job vacancies, and the data is not available and probably will not be available until the end of the year.
Additionally, as far as another survey is concerned the minister told the House a few days ago that he is spending I do not know how many dollars on it, this time collecting data on occupational shortages. I do not know what is the difference between job vacancies and occupational shortages but I suppose that some sophisticated bureaucrat in the department, even the minister himself, being a former law professor, may be able to argue the difference between the two. The fact of the matter is, however, that the difference does not really matter to the man who is out of work, which should be the key purpose of the department to remedy.
Another statistical analysis undertaken by the department relates to job orders. Here again, I do not know how much money is involved because the amount has not yet been determined. Looking at some statistics in this regard, in the fiscal year 1966-67 employers placed 850,000 job orders with Canada Manpower. By the last fiscal year, 1970-71, it had dropped to fewer than 600,000.
There is another statistical series which has emanated from the minister's department, namely, job placements by Canada Manpower. Not surprisingly, the statistical figures for this operation are equally disastrous. In the period 1965-66, when we still had the National Employment Service in operation and a much smaller labour force than we have today, the number of placements by the department was 961,000. In the last fiscal, 1970-71, the number of placements by the new department working under extended operations had fallen to below 650,000, a drop of some 32 per cent in job placements.
I think more pertinent than that is the fact that in 1965-66 the cost of placing a person in a job was $23. Today, taking into account manpower training and all the other programs of the department, the cost of placing one person in a job has escalated to $647. If we exclude the training program, it still costs about $268 to place a person in a job. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) and all the other ministers, obsessed as they are with destroying and defeating inflation, cannot be accused of losing the battle at such a clip as to account for the 2,700 per cent increase in placement costs over only five years.
In the field of the operations of the Department of Manpower and Immigration three things only are growing: one, the amount of money being spent; two, the number of bureaucrats being employed by the department and, three, the number of people who are unemployed in the nation. These three factors do not make up any equation at all. The growth in these areas seems to be
October 21, 1971

the only accomplishment of the department. I think the statistic-and the minister seems to be obsessed with statistics-which the minister should be giving to the public is how many of the people who actually go through manpower training end up getting jobs afterwards. How many are successful? The manpower training program is currently costing over $300 million a year, and another $35 million was added to that figure the other day.
What is it for? Primarily, to train people for jobs that simply do not exist. I think the main objective, therefore, in the eyes of the government is to hide away, to cover up in any given month some 80,000 unemployed people so that the forecasts and prognostications of the Minister of Finance about the level of unemployment will look slightly less ludicrous and damaging than they otherwise would. I personally, members of this House and people across the country object strongly to that sort of government trickery and I resent very much the cruelty of the hoax which is being perpetrated on the unemployed. Quite a number of them hope that after the training is over there will be a job waiting for them. Regretfully, that does not seem to be the case.
The minister has made a mess in his handling of the grain situation. It appears that he is bent on making an equal mess of the manpower aspect that is under his jurisdiction.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the hon. member and, in my reply, I shall try to disregard the partisan side of his remarks-

Mr. Speaker, may I deal with the matter the hon. member has raised. With respect to that part of the hon. member's question relating to the job vacancy survey, I would point out that this survey is being conducted among employers throughout Canada in the expectation that the results will give a more constant picture of the state of the labour market at the national level. Particular attention is being paid to those job vacancies which have been open for a month or more, and the survey will produce a three-month moving average of these vacancies.
However, as was pointed out to the hon. member, the survey is still in the developmental stage. As this job
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion vacancy survey is being developed by Statistics Canada under contract to the Department of Manpower and Immigration, I would suggest that if more technical information is required relating to the timing of completion of this developmental work such a request should be directed to the minister responsible for Statistics Canada. The development of this survey is but one aspect of a continuing effort to improve the quality of labour market knowledge available to assist in the planning and implementation of manpower programs and placement activities.
With specific reference to the hon. member's remarks concerning the job placement activities of the department, I would point out that the main reason there has been a decline in the number of placements in employment by Canada Manpower centres since 1965 and 1966 is that Canada Manpower centres have been heavily involved in several new programs and services which have been added to the functions performed by the Canada Manpower centres, including the Canada Manpower training program and the Canada Manpower mobility program. When the placements in these programs are taken into account, the total output of the Canada Manpower centres compares favourably with previous years. I say that because I believe it is the answer the hon. member is looking for. For example, in 1970-71 the Canada Manpower centres placed 344,846 people in training and made 648,966 placements in jobs, excluding casual jobs, for a total of 993,812. This total exceeds the 960,995 placements made in 1965-66.
